guidelines.guideline: AHA/ASA 2021 Secondary Prevention; CHANCE / POINT / THALES / INSPIRES
guidelines.statement: In patients with minor non-cardioembolic ischemic stroke (NIHSS ≤3 or ≤5 with disabling deficit) or high-risk TIA (ABCD² ≥4 or DWI+), dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin plus clopidogrel for 21 days, or aspirin plus ticagrelor for 30 days) started within 24 h is recommended to reduce recurrent ischemic stroke at 90 days.
caveats: Duration is indication-specific. For THIS indication (minor stroke / high-risk TIA) the trial-supported courses are aspirin+clopidogrel 21 days or aspirin+ticagrelor 30 days; do not extend beyond 30 days.

A separate indication permits longer DAPT: severe intracranial stenosis 70-99% within 30 days of the event allows aspirin+clopidogrel up to 90 days. Beyond 90 days, or triple antiplatelet therapy, carries excess hemorrhage risk. Source of truth for both bounds: src/guidelines/secondary-prevention-2021.json.
INSPIRES extended the window to 72 h in eligible mild stroke / high-risk TIA.
For CYP2C19 loss-of-function carriers, ticagrelor (CHANCE-2) is preferred over clopidogrel.

guidelines.guideline: AHA/ASA 2021 Secondary Prevention; OPTIMAS (2024); CATALYST IPDMA (2025); ELAN (2023); TIMING (2022)
guidelines.statement: In patients with AIS and atrial fibrillation, early DOAC initiation within ~4 days is reasonable across stroke severities (OPTIMAS: non-inferior across infarct sizes) and was superior to delayed start at 30 days in pooled individual-patient data (CATALYST IPDMA: OR 0.70, 95% CI 0.50-0.98, no sICH excess), excepting very severe stroke or extensive hemorrhagic transformation.
caveats: Reserve longer delay for very severe stroke or extensive hemorrhagic transformation; confirm absence of significant hemorrhagic transformation on follow-up imaging before starting in moderate-large stroke.
Early initiation (≤4 d) is non-inferior across severities (OPTIMAS) and superior at 30 d in pooled IPD (CATALYST); individualize for the highest-risk presentations.

Scope note: this COR IIa statement covers the early-start question. The wider 2-14 day window carries a separate, weaker COR IIb statement — the two are not in conflict. Source of truth: src/guidelines/secondary-prevention-2021.json.

guidelines.statement: In acute spontaneous ICH, continuous smooth, sustained BP control with timely treatment can be beneficial when BP lowering is indicated.
caveats: Smooth, sustained BP control and timely treatment are Class IIa process recommendations.
Do not present INTERACT3 as BP-only class evidence; it tested a bundle including BP, glucose, temperature, and anticoagulation reversal.
Avoid abrupt large drops in BP (>60 mmHg) which may worsen outcomes.
Do not pursue a numeric BP target in isolation from neurologic status and the full care bundle.

guidelines.statement: In mild-to-moderate acute spontaneous ICH with presenting SBP 150-220 mmHg, targeting SBP 140 mmHg and maintaining 130-150 mmHg when appropriate is safe and may be reasonable.
caveats: The SBP 140/range 130-150 target is Class IIb.
In patients with SBP >220 mmHg, the safety of aggressive lowering to 140 is less certain; use clinical judgment and continuous monitoring.
Use with the separate Class IIa process recommendation for smooth, sustained control and timely treatment.
Do not pursue a numeric BP target in isolation from neurologic status, hematoma severity, and neurosurgical planning.

guidelines.statement: Avoid acute SBP <130 mmHg in mild-to-moderate spontaneous ICH because it is potentially harmful.
caveats: Acute SBP <130 mmHg is Class III-harm.
This lower-bound harm guard is separate from the Class IIb SBP 140/range 130-150 target.

guidelines.statement: In factor Xa inhibitor-associated ICH within 15 hours of last dose, andexanet alfa is reasonable to achieve hemostatic efficacy when available; 4F-PCC is an alternative when andexanet is unavailable or contraindicated. Monitor for thrombotic complications.
caveats: ANNEXA-I demonstrated higher hemostatic efficacy with andexanet but more thrombotic complications vs usual care.
Andexanet alfa is not indicated for edoxaban; for edoxaban, 4F-PCC remains primary.
Reversal should not delay neurosurgical evaluation.

guidelines.statement: In warfarin-associated ICH, give vitamin K 10 mg IV plus 4F-PCC dosed by INR/weight to rapidly reverse anticoagulation; FFP is an inferior alternative.
caveats: Vitamin K is required for sustained reversal; PCC alone is short-acting.
FFP carries volume-overload risk and slower correction.

guidelines.statement: In patients presenting 4.5-9 h from LKW or with wake-up stroke, IV thrombolysis (alteplase or tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg) selected by perfusion or DWI-FLAIR mismatch is reasonable when EVT is not indicated or available.
caveats: Imaging-based selection is required; unselected late-window thrombolysis is not supported (TWIST).
Time from LKW remains a key safety determinant; TIMELESS extended TNK to 24 h with mismatch selection but the overall primary endpoint did not reach significance.

guidelines.statement: In patients with anterior-circulation LVO and ASPECTS 3-5 (or core 50-100 mL) within 24 h of LKW, EVT is recommended to improve functional outcome.
caveats: Pre-stroke mRS, life expectancy, and goals of care still inform shared decision-making.

Very low ASPECTS is not unaddressed: ASPECTS 0-2 within 6 h and ASPECTS 0-5 within 0-6 h both carry recommendations, each bounded by age 18-80 and pre-stroke mRS 0-1. Those age and mRS limits are part of the recommendation and are easy to drop when quoting the ASPECTS number alone. Source of truth: src/guidelines/ais-2026.json.

guidelines.statement: In patients with anterior-circulation LVO presenting 6-24 h from LKW, EVT is recommended for those meeting DAWN or DEFUSE-3 imaging-selection criteria.
caveats: Outside trial-selection criteria, EVT is reasonable on a case-by-case basis with shared decision-making.

guidelines.statement: Tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg (max 25 mg) is a reasonable alternative to alteplase 0.9 mg/kg for IV thrombolysis in eligible AIS within 4.5 h, particularly for patients with anticipated EVT.
caveats: Use TNK 0.25 mg/kg only; the 0.4 mg/kg dose was not non-inferior in EXTEND-IA TNK part 2.
Local protocols may continue to favor alteplase; both are acceptable.

trials.name: RESCUE BT2
trials.fullName: Tirofiban for Stroke without Large or Medium-Sized Vessel Occlusion
trials.population: n=1177, adults, NIHSS NIHSS ≥5 with at least one moderately-to-severely weak limb, four entry routes: ≤24 h and ineligible for reperfusion; progression at 24-96 h; early deterioration after thrombolysis; or no improvement 4-24 h after thrombolysis
trials.finding: Favors tirofiban: 29.1% vs 22.2%
trials.teachingPoint: IV tirofiban improved 90-day excellent outcome in non-occlusive, often progressive stroke, with inconsistent secondary endpoints.

trials.name: ATTRACTION
trials.fullName: Adjunct Tirofiban Treatment after Successful Endovascular Thrombectomy Recanalisation in Acute Anterior Circulation Ischaemic Stroke
trials.population: n=1380, median 71 y (IQR 62-77); 591 (43%) female, 789 (57%) male, NIHSS not restricted by a protocol NIHSS band (anterior-circulation LVO), Randomization after successful reperfusion by thrombectomy
trials.finding: MET superiority, favoring tirofiban: 49% (340/689) vs 43% (299/691)
trials.teachingPoint: Reopens the adjunctive-antiplatelet question specifically for the post-reperfusion window, while the numerically higher symptomatic haemorrhage and the near-uniformly Han Chinese cohort mean it is not yet a general recommendation.

trials.name: RESCUE BT
trials.fullName: Effect of Intravenous Tirofiban vs Placebo Before Endovascular Thrombectomy on Functional Outcomes in Large Vessel Occlusion Stroke
trials.population: n=948, mean 67 y; 391 (41.2%) women, NIHSS not restricted by a protocol NIHSS band (proximal intracranial LVO), ≤24 h from time last known well
trials.finding: DID NOT meet superiority — neutral: median (IQR) 90-day mRS 3 (1-4) with tirofiban vs 3 (1-4) with placebo
trials.teachingPoint: Does not support giving intravenous tirofiban before endovascular thrombectomy: 90-day disability was unchanged and symptomatic hemorrhage was numerically higher.

trials.name: MOST
trials.fullName: Multi-arm Optimization of Stroke Thrombolysis: Adjunctive Intravenous Argatroban or Eptifibatide for Ischemic Stroke
trials.population: n=514, adults ≥18 y, NIHSS NIHSS ≥6 before intravenous thrombolysis, IV thrombolysis within 3 h of onset; study drug started within 75 min of the start of thrombolysis
trials.finding: DID NOT meet superiority for either adjunct — mean (±SD) utility-weighted 90-day mRS 5.2±3.7 with argatroban, 6.3±3.2 with eptifibatide and 6.8±3.0 with placebo; both adjuncts were numerically WORSE than placebo
trials.teachingPoint: Argues against adding intravenous argatroban or eptifibatide to IV thrombolysis in the first hours after treatment: no reduction in disability, and a numerical mortality excess the trial was stopped too early to characterise.

trials.name: DIRECT ANGIO
trials.fullName: Direct versus Conventional Transfer to Angiography Suite in Patients with Severe Acute Stroke Treated with Thrombectomy (France)
trials.population: n=115, ≤85, ≤5 h of onset
trials.finding: No benefit: 36% vs 42%
trials.teachingPoint: Bypassing pre-EVT imaging increased sICH without benefit and was halted early — cautions against direct-to-angio in suspected LVO.

trials.name: ESCAPE-NA1
trials.fullName: Efficacy and safety of nerinetide for the treatment of acute ischaemic stroke (ESCAPE-NA1): a multicentre, double-blind, randomised controlled trial
trials.population: n=1105, ≥18 y (median not reported in the abstract), NIHSS Disabling ischaemic stroke at randomisation; no numeric NIHSS threshold specified in the abstract, ≤12 h from onset
trials.finding: DID NOT meet: mRS 0-2 in 337/549 (61.4%) with nerinetide vs 329/556 (59.2%) with placebo
trials.teachingPoint: Establishes that adding a PSD-95 inhibitor to thrombectomy did not improve 90-day function, and frames why no acute neuroprotectant has entered routine practice.

trials.name: ESCAPE-NEXT
trials.fullName: Efficacy and safety of nerinetide in acute ischaemic stroke in patients undergoing endovascular thrombectomy without previous thrombolysis (ESCAPE-NEXT): a multicentre, double-blind, randomised controlled trial
trials.population: n=850, ≥18 y (median not reported in the abstract), NIHSS NIHSS >5 (disabling stroke at randomisation), ≤12 h from onset
trials.finding: DID NOT meet: mRS 0-2 in 206/454 (45%) with nerinetide vs 181/396 (46%) with placebo — no benefit, with the point estimate very slightly favouring placebo
trials.teachingPoint: Closes the nerinetide question for thrombectomy without thrombolysis: there is no functional benefit, and no basis for using it outside a trial.

trials.name: ACTISAVE
trials.fullName: Glenzocimab Efficacy and Safety Added to Intravenous Thrombolysis With or Without Mechanical Thrombectomy in Patients With Acute Ischemic Stroke — ACTISAVE: A Prospective, Randomized, Double-Blind Study
trials.population: n=438, Median 73 y (IQR 63-80); 43% female, NIHSS Median pre-thrombolysis NIHSS 9 (IQR 6-15), Thrombolysis within 4.5 h of onset (median 2.3 h); study drug started a median of 1.2 h [IQR 0.8-1.6] after thrombolysis initiation
trials.finding: DID NOT meet: poor outcome in 21.6% with glenzocimab vs 15.3% with placebo — not significant, and the point estimate numerically favours placebo
trials.teachingPoint: Glenzocimab is not an established adjunct to thrombolysis; the trial that was meant to confirm benefit did not, and there is no bedside role outside research.

trials.name: TASTE (edaravone dexborneol)
trials.fullName: Edaravone Dexborneol Versus Edaravone Alone for the Treatment of Acute Ischemic Stroke: A Phase III, Randomized, Double-Blind, Comparative Trial
trials.population: n=1165, 35-80 y, NIHSS NIHSS 4-24, ≤48 h from onset
trials.finding: MET: mRS ≤1 in 67.18% with edaravone dexborneol vs 58.97% with edaravone alone — the combination was superior to edaravone alone
trials.teachingPoint: Explains why edaravone dexborneol is used routinely in China and why that practice has not transferred: the trial's control arm was edaravone, not placebo or usual care.

trials.name: TASTE-2
trials.fullName: Edaravone dexborneol versus placebo on functional outcomes in patients with acute ischaemic stroke undergoing endovascular thrombectomy (TASTE-2): randomised controlled trial
trials.population: n=1362, 18-80 y, NIHSS NIHSS 6-25, ≤24 h from symptom onset
trials.finding: Nominally MET but only just: mRS 0-2 in 379/689 (55.0%) with edaravone dexborneol vs 333/671 (49.6%) with placebo; risk difference 5.4% (95% CI 0.1% to 10.7%). The lower bound of the risk-ratio confidence interval sits exactly at 1.00 and P=0.05, so this is a borderline rather than a robust result
trials.teachingPoint: The best current signal that a cytoprotectant may add something to thrombectomy — borderline, single-country and not yet a basis for routine use.

trials.name: EMPHASIS
trials.fullName: Efficacy and safety of minocycline in patients with acute ischaemic stroke (EMPHASIS): a multicentre, double-blind, randomised controlled trial
trials.population: n=1724, Median 65 y (IQR 57-71); 1151 (66.8%) male, 573 (33.2%) female, NIHSS Entry range NIHSS 4-25 with level-of-consciousness subscale (1a) ≤1, but MEDIAN BASELINE NIHSS WAS 5 (IQR 4-7) — a predominantly mild-stroke cohort, ≤72 h from onset
trials.finding: MET: mRS 0-1 in 447/850 (52.6%) with minocycline vs 403/851 (47.4%) with placebo — a 5.2 percentage-point absolute difference favouring minocycline
trials.teachingPoint: The strongest positive neuroprotection signal to date, but in a mild-stroke Chinese cohort awaiting replication — not yet a reason to give minocycline outside a trial.

trials.name: MIST-A
trials.fullName: Efficacy and safety of minocycline on patients with acute anterior circulation ischaemic stroke undergoing mechanical thrombectomy (MIST-A): a multicentre, prospective, randomised, open-label, blinded-endpoint, phase 2 trial
trials.population: n=189, Not reported in the abstract, NIHSS Not reported in the abstract, After mechanical thrombectomy with successful recanalisation
trials.finding: DID NOT meet: median infarct growth ratio 1.8 (IQR 1.3-3.3) with minocycline vs 1.6 (IQR 1.2-2.8) with standard care — no reduction in infarct growth, with the point estimate numerically favouring the control arm
trials.teachingPoint: Shows minocycline does not limit infarct growth after successful thrombectomy, and keeps the positive EMPHASIS result from being generalised to reperfused large-vessel stroke.

trials.name: AVERROES
trials.fullName: Apixaban in Patients with Atrial Fibrillation Unsuitable for VKA
trials.population: n=5599, ≥50, NIHSS n/a, chronic AF
trials.finding: Favored apixaban: 1.6%/y vs 3.7%/y
trials.teachingPoint: Supports anticoagulation over aspirin for AF stroke prevention generally; the ICH-survivor question is answered by the dedicated trials below.

trials.name: PRESTIGE-AF
trials.fullName: Prevention of Stroke in Intracerebral Haemorrhage Survivors with Atrial Fibrillation
trials.population: n=319, median 79, NIHSS n/a, Spontaneous ICH survivors with AF, mRS ≤4
trials.finding: Ischaemic stroke markedly reduced (0.83 vs 8.60 per 100 patient-years); recurrent ICH did NOT meet non-inferiority (5.00 vs 0.82 per 100 patient-years)
trials.teachingPoint: Objective: anticoagulation after ICH in AF trades a large ischaemic-stroke reduction against a substantial recurrent-ICH increase; individualize.

trials.name: ENRICH-AF
trials.fullName: Edoxaban for Intracranial Hemorrhage Survivors with Atrial Fibrillation
trials.population: n=948, ≥45, NIHSS n/a, Intracranial-haemorrhage survivors with high-risk AF (CHA₂DS₂-VASc ≥2)
trials.finding: Full efficacy not yet reported; the lobar-ICH subgroup was stopped by the DSMB for excess recurrent haemorrhagic stroke
trials.teachingPoint: Objective: interim DSMB stopped edoxaban in lobar ICH for excess rebleeding; the main efficacy comparison is awaited.

trials.name: SoSTART
trials.fullName: Start or Stop Anticoagulants Randomised Trial
trials.population: n=203, adults, NIHSS n/a, Survivors of spontaneous intracranial haemorrhage with AF (CHA₂DS₂-VASc ≥2)
trials.finding: Inconclusive: 8/101 (8%) start vs 4/102 (4%) avoid; starting NOT shown non-inferior
trials.teachingPoint: Objective: did not establish non-inferiority of starting anticoagulation after ICH; hypothesis-generating.

trials.name: APACHE-AF
trials.fullName: Apixaban After Anticoagulation-Associated Intracerebral Haemorrhage in Atrial Fibrillation
trials.population: n=101, median 78, NIHSS n/a, 7-90 d after anticoagulation-associated ICH; AF, CHA₂DS₂-VASc ≥2, mRS ≤4
trials.finding: No difference: 26% (12.6%/y) apixaban vs 24% (11.9%/y) avoid; high absolute risk in both arms
trials.teachingPoint: Objective: no clear difference; both strategies carry high residual vascular risk.

trials.name: COCROACH
trials.fullName: Oral Anticoagulation after Intracranial Haemorrhage in AF: Individual-Patient-Data Meta-analysis
trials.population: n=412, 75% ≥75, NIHSS n/a, AF with prior spontaneous intracranial haemorrhage (pooled RCTs: SoSTART, APACHE-AF, NASPAF-ICH, and the ICH subgroup of ELDERCARE-AF)
trials.finding: Favoured anticoagulation but non-significant: 14% vs 22%
trials.teachingPoint: Objective synthesis: net benefit of anticoagulation after ICH in AF remains statistically uncertain; ischaemic reduction is offset by a non-significant bleeding increase.

trials.name: ELAN
trials.fullName: Early versus Later Anticoagulation for Stroke with Atrial Fibrillation
trials.population: n=2013, ≥18, NIHSS all, post-AIS, ≤28 d
trials.finding: 2.9% (early) vs 4.1% (later)
trials.teachingPoint: Supports early DOAC initiation per stroke severity.

trials.name: TIMING
trials.fullName: Timing of Oral Anticoagulant Therapy in AIS with AF
trials.population: n=888, ≥18, NIHSS all, ≤72 h post-AIS
trials.finding: Non-inferior: 6.89% (early) vs 8.68% (delayed)
trials.teachingPoint: Supports earlier DOAC initiation.

trials.name: OPTIMAS
trials.fullName: Optimal Timing of Anticoagulation after Acute Ischaemic Stroke with Atrial Fibrillation
trials.population: n=3621, ≥18, Early ≤4 d vs delayed 7-14 d
trials.finding: Non-inferior: 3.3% vs 3.3%
trials.teachingPoint: Early DOAC (≤4 d) non-inferior to delayed — do not routinely delay anticoagulation.

trials.name: CATALYST
trials.fullName: IPD Meta-analysis of Anticoagulation Timing after Ischaemic Stroke with AF
trials.population: n=5441, Early ≤4 d vs later ≥5 d
trials.finding: Favored early: 2.1% vs 3.0%
trials.teachingPoint: Pooled IPD shows early DOAC (≤4 d) reduces 30-d composite — supports early initiation.

trials.name: STABLED
trials.fullName: Catheter Ablation and Oral Anticoagulation for Secondary Stroke Prevention in Atrial Fibrillation
trials.population: n=249, 20-85 (mean 71.7), Ablation 1-6 mo after index stroke
trials.finding: No reduction: 5.6% vs 4.9% per person-year
trials.teachingPoint: Adding ablation to anticoagulation did not reduce recurrent events in post-stroke AF (underpowered) — does not support routine ablation for secondary prevention.

trials.name: ISAT (18-year)
trials.fullName: Durability of Endovascular Coiling versus Neurosurgical Clipping of Ruptured Cerebral Aneurysms — 18-year follow-up of the UK ISAT cohort
trials.population: n=1644, adults, NIHSS treatment equipoise between clipping and coiling, randomized 1994-2002; followed 10.0-18.5 years
trials.finding: Favors coiling: alive and independent more likely after coiling
trials.teachingPoint: Coiling retains a survival and disability-free-survival advantage over clipping at 10+ years when both are feasible.

trials.name: CATIS
trials.fullName: China Antihypertensive Trial in Acute Ischemic Stroke
trials.population: n=4071, adults (age range not stated in the primary report), NIHSS not reported in the primary report, ≤48 h from onset
trials.finding: NULL - the primary outcome DID NOT differ between groups: 683 events with antihypertensive treatment vs 681 events with control
trials.teachingPoint: Teaches that lowering BP in the first 24-48 h of non-thrombolysed ischaemic stroke is comorbidity management rather than a neuroprotective intervention - it changed neither death nor disability.

trials.name: CATIS-2
trials.fullName: China Antihypertensive Trial in Acute Ischaemic Stroke II - early versus delayed antihypertensive treatment in patients with acute ischaemic stroke
trials.population: n=4810, ≥40 years, NIHSS mild-to-moderate stroke (severity distribution not given in the primary report), enrolled 24-48 h after symptom onset
trials.finding: NULL - early treatment DID NOT reduce dependency or death: 289/2413 (12.0%) early vs 250/2397 (10.5%) delayed. The point estimate numerically favours delaying treatment.
trials.teachingPoint: Supports not rushing to restart or start antihypertensives in the first week after a non-thrombolysed ischaemic stroke - deferring to day 8 was not worse at 90 days.

trials.name: ENOS
trials.fullName: Efficacy of Nitric Oxide, With or Without Continuing Antihypertensive Treatment, for Management of High Blood Pressure in Acute Stroke - a partial-factorial randomised controlled trial
trials.population: n=4011, adults admitted to hospital with acute stroke (age range not stated in the primary report), NIHSS not reported in the primary report, within 48 h of stroke onset (median 26 h, IQR 16-37)
trials.finding: NULL in BOTH comparisons - functional outcome DID NOT differ for glyceryl trinitrate versus none, nor for continuing versus stopping pre-stroke antihypertensives
trials.teachingPoint: The authors state there is no evidence to support continuing pre-stroke antihypertensive drugs in the first few days after acute stroke - the decision to hold or continue does not change 90-day function.

trials.name: COSSACS
trials.fullName: Continue or Stop Post-Stroke Antihypertensives Collaborative Study
trials.population: n=763, >18 years, NIHSS predominantly mild stroke (the investigators describe the cohort as acute mild stroke); NIHSS distribution not reported, enrolled within 48 h of stroke AND within 48 h of the last antihypertensive dose
trials.finding: NULL - continuing antihypertensives DID NOT reduce death or dependency: 72/379 continue vs 82/384 stop
trials.teachingPoint: Adds a safety argument to the continue-or-stop discussion: the lower pressures produced by continuing home antihypertensives after mild stroke were not associated with more adverse events, though the trial was too small to settle the efficacy question.

trials.name: SCAST
trials.fullName: Scandinavian Candesartan Acute Stroke Trial - the angiotensin-receptor blocker candesartan for treatment of acute stroke
trials.population: n=2029, older than 18 years, NIHSS not reported in the primary report (Scandinavian Stroke Scale used as a secondary outcome), within 30 h of symptom onset
trials.finding: NEITHER co-primary favoured candesartan. The composite vascular endpoint did not differ (120 events candesartan vs 111 placebo). Functional outcome trended WORSE with candesartan, but the trend DID NOT clear the prespecified p≤0.025 threshold, so it is a signal rather than a demonstration of harm.
trials.teachingPoint: Argues against reflexively starting an ARB for BP lowering within 30 h of acute stroke - the functional trend went the wrong way and symptomatic hypotension and renal failure were numerically more common.

trials.name: CHASE
trials.fullName: Controlling Hypertension After Severe Cerebrovascular Event - a randomized, multicenter, controlled study
trials.population: n=500, adults (age range not stated in the primary report), NIHSS acute SEVERE stroke; severity scale distribution not reported, acute phase of severe stroke
trials.finding: NULL - individualized lowering DID NOT significantly reduce poor outcome: 71.1% vs 73.4%. The point estimate numerically favours individualization but the confidence interval is wide and includes both meaningful benefit and meaningful harm.
trials.teachingPoint: Shows that in severe stroke an individualized 10-15% BP reduction did not clearly beat a permissive fixed ceiling, and that outcomes remained poor in about 72% of patients regardless of strategy.

trials.name: Early AHT in AIS meta-analysis
trials.fullName: Early antihypertensive therapy in acute ischemic stroke: a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
trials.population: n=15521, adults enrolled in the component randomized trials, NIHSS not reported at the meta-analysis level, antihypertensive therapy initiated within 48 h of symptom onset
trials.finding: NULL on both primary outcomes - early antihypertensive therapy was NOT associated with a difference in all-cause mortality or in death/functional dependency
trials.teachingPoint: Provides the one-line summary for the category: early BP lowering in acute ischaemic stroke produces a real BP reduction and no measurable change in mortality, dependency or recurrence.

trials.name: ENCHANTED2/MT
trials.fullName: Intensive BP Control after Endovascular Thrombectomy
trials.population: n=821, ≥18, NIHSS all, post-successful EVT
trials.finding: Favored less-intensive (worse with intensive)
trials.teachingPoint: Avoid intensive BP lowering after successful EVT; target 140-180 mmHg.

trials.name: OPTIMAL-BP
trials.fullName: Intensive vs Conventional Blood Pressure Lowering after Successful Endovascular Thrombectomy
trials.population: n=306, ≥18, NIHSS all, After successful EVT (mTICI ≥2b)
trials.finding: Intensive worse: 39.4% vs 54.4%
trials.teachingPoint: Intensive SBP <140 after successful EVT reduced functional independence; reinforces ENCHANTED2/MT.

trials.name: BP-TARGET
trials.fullName: Safety and efficacy of intensive blood pressure lowering after successful endovascular therapy in acute ischaemic stroke (BP-TARGET)
trials.population: n=324, adults ≥18 years, NIHSS not reported in the primary report, target achieved within 1 h of randomisation and maintained for 24 h after reperfusion
trials.finding: NULL - the intensive target DID NOT reduce radiographic intraparenchymal haemorrhage: 65/154 (42%) intensive vs 68/157 (43%) standard
trials.teachingPoint: Establishes that driving SBP to 100-129 mm Hg after successful thrombectomy does not reduce post-procedural intraparenchymal haemorrhage - it removed the main mechanistic rationale for intensive lowering before the later trials showed functional harm.

trials.name: BEST-II
trials.fullName: Blood Pressure Management After Endovascular Therapy for Acute Ischemic Stroke: The BEST-II Randomized Clinical Trial
trials.population: n=120, mean 69.6 years (SD 14.5); 69 of 120 (58%) female, NIHSS not reported in the primary report, targets initiated within 60 minutes of recanalization and maintained for 24 h
trials.finding: DID NOT meet the prespecified futility criteria. Mean follow-up infarct volume was 32.4 mL for the <140 mm Hg group, 50.7 mL for the <160 mm Hg group and 46.4 mL for the ≤180 mm Hg group - the MOST intensive arm had the SMALLEST infarct volume. Mean utility-weighted mRS was 0.51 (<140), 0.47 (<160) and 0.58 (≤180). This is a low probability of benefit, NOT demonstrated harm.
trials.teachingPoint: Teaches the difference between 'low probability of future trial success' and 'demonstrated harm' - and supplies the reason the ≤180 mm Hg ceiling, rather than a 140-160 band, remains the referenced target after thrombectomy.

trials.name: IDENTIFY
trials.fullName: Early intensive blood pressure management after endovascular treatment in ischaemic stroke (IDENTIFY): a multicentre, open-label, blinded-endpoint, randomised controlled trial
trials.population: n=383, adults (age range not stated in the primary report), NIHSS not reported in the primary report, endovascular treatment within 6 h of onset; blood-pressure targets maintained until 24 h post-EVT
trials.finding: NULL - intensive management to <130 mm Hg DID NOT improve outcomes: 130/183 (71.0%) intensive vs 135/200 (67.5%) standard
trials.teachingPoint: Adds a third randomised null to the post-thrombectomy BP question - a <130 mm Hg target within the 6-hour window changed neither function, haemorrhage, oedema nor death.

trials.name: OPTIMAL-BP 1-year
trials.fullName: Intensive Versus Conventional Blood Pressure Lowering After Successful Endovascular Thrombectomy: OPTIMAL-BP 1-Year Outcomes
trials.population: n=306, adults (age range not stated in the extension report; age was an adjustment covariate), NIHSS baseline NIHSS used as an adjustment covariate; distribution not reported in the extension, randomisation within 2 h after recanalization; BP targets applied for 24 h after enrolment; follow-up extended to 1 year
trials.finding: Functional independence at 1 year was NUMERICALLY LOWER with intensive management (40.5% vs 52.7%), but the INTENTION-TO-TREAT estimate did NOT cross conventional significance (P=0.051). Only the per-protocol analysis did (41.1% vs 54.7%, P=0.040). State this as persistence of the early signal, not as newly proven long-term harm, and never quote the per-protocol figure as if it were the intention-to-treat result.
trials.teachingPoint: Shows the functional cost of 24 hours of intensive post-thrombectomy BP lowering is still measurable at one year, reinforcing existing recommendations against intensive lowering after successful reperfusion.

trials.name: Cochrane review: BP after reperfusion
trials.fullName: Blood pressure management in reperfused ischemic stroke (Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews)
trials.population: n=4381, adults enrolled in the included randomized trials, NIHSS NIHSS pooled as an outcome, not an inclusion criterion, blood-pressure management during and after reperfusion by systemic thrombolysis or endovascular thrombectomy
trials.finding: Intensive management results in LITTLE TO NO clinically meaningful difference in clinical function (high-certainty evidence). IMPORTANT READING NOTE: the published abstract does not state the direction of the mRS dichotomy, so this risk ratio must NOT be paraphrased as favouring either arm.
trials.teachingPoint: Supplies the GRADE-graded bottom line for post-reperfusion BP: intensive systolic lowering below 160 mm Hg buys no clinically meaningful functional benefit and probably increases all-cause mortality.

trials.name: ESPRIT (BP)
trials.fullName: Lowering Systolic Blood Pressure to <120 mm Hg versus <140 mm Hg in Patients at High Cardiovascular Risk
trials.population: n=11255, mean 64.6 ± 7.1, NIHSS high cardiovascular risk; 4359 with diabetes and 3022 with previous stroke, median 3.4 years
trials.finding: Favors intensive: 9.7% vs 11.1%
trials.teachingPoint: An SBP target <120 reduced major vascular events versus <140, with consistent benefit in patients with diabetes and prior stroke.

trials.name: BPROAD
trials.fullName: Intensive Blood-Pressure Control in Patients with Type 2 Diabetes
trials.population: n=12821, >=50 (mean 63.8 ± 7.5); 45.3% women, NIHSS type 2 diabetes with elevated SBP and increased cardiovascular risk, median 4.2 years
trials.finding: Favors intensive: 1.65 vs 2.09 events per 100 person-years
trials.teachingPoint: In type 2 diabetes, an SBP target <120 cut major cardiovascular events by 21% versus <140, at the cost of more hypotension and hyperkalemia.

trials.name: IRIS IPD meta-analysis
trials.fullName: Value of intravenous thrombolysis in endovascular treatment for large-vessel anterior circulation stroke: individual participant data meta-analysis of six randomised trials (IRIS)
trials.population: n=2313, adults; pooled from six randomised trials, NIHSS large-vessel anterior-circulation occlusion, IVT-eligible time windows of the six contributing trials
trials.finding: DID NOT establish non-inferiority of EVT alone: median mRS 3 (IQR 1-5) with EVT alone vs 2 (IQR 1-4) with IVT plus EVT. The CI crosses both the 0.82 non-inferiority boundary and 1.00, so this is an INDETERMINATE result — it neither establishes non-inferiority of skipping the lytic nor demonstrates superiority of bridging.
trials.teachingPoint: Teaches the difference between a negative trial and an inconclusive one: the pooled data cannot exclude a meaningful loss of benefit from skipping the lytic, which is why bridging remained the default for an IVT-eligible patient presenting directly to a thrombectomy centre.

trials.name: IRIS time-dependency analysis
trials.fullName: Time to Treatment With Intravenous Thrombolysis Before Thrombectomy and Functional Outcomes in Acute Ischemic Stroke: A Meta-Analysis
trials.population: n=2313, median 71 years (IQR 62-78); 44.3% female, NIHSS anterior-circulation large-vessel occlusion (2313 of 2334 pooled participants), median time from symptom onset to EXPECTED administration of IVT 2 h 28 min (IQR 1 h 46 min to 3 h 17 min)
trials.finding: Statistically significant interaction: the benefit of adding IVT falls as the interval from onset to expected IVT lengthens. Adjusted common OR for a 1-step mRS shift toward improvement 1.49 at 1 hour, 1.25 at 2 hours, 1.04 at 3 hours.
trials.teachingPoint: Reframes the bridging debate as a clock question rather than a yes/no question: the added value of a lytic before thrombectomy is large very early and shrinks toward nothing by roughly two and a half hours from onset — a gradient, not a threshold.

trials.name: DIRECT-MT
trials.fullName: Endovascular Thrombectomy with or without Intravenous Alteplase in Acute Stroke
trials.population: n=656, adults, NIHSS acute ischaemic stroke from anterior-circulation large-vessel occlusion, alteplase administered within 4.5 h of symptom onset
trials.finding: MET non-inferiority within its prespecified 0.8 margin: thrombectomy alone was non-inferior to alteplase plus thrombectomy. The authors' own conclusion states this holds 'within a 20% margin of confidence.'
trials.teachingPoint: The canonical worked example of why a non-inferiority margin must be read before the conclusion — a 'non-inferior' label that tolerates a 20% relative loss of benefit is a different claim from equivalence.

trials.name: SKIP
trials.fullName: Effect of Mechanical Thrombectomy Without vs With Intravenous Thrombolysis on Functional Outcome Among Patients With Acute Ischemic Stroke: The SKIP Randomized Clinical Trial
trials.population: n=204, median 74 years; 62.7% men, NIHSS median NIHSS 18, IVT-eligible acute large-vessel occlusion; enrolment January 2017 to July 2019, final follow-up October 2019
trials.finding: DID NOT demonstrate non-inferiority: 60/101 (59.4%) with thrombectomy alone vs 59/103 (57.3%) with low-dose alteplase plus thrombectomy. The authors explicitly add that the wide confidence intervals also did NOT allow a conclusion of inferiority — an inconclusive trial, not a negative one.
trials.teachingPoint: Illustrates that an underpowered non-inferiority trial answers nothing — SKIP excluded neither benefit nor harm from omitting the lytic, and its comparator was Japan's low-dose alteplase, not the 0.9 mg/kg used elsewhere.

trials.name: DEVT
trials.fullName: Effect of Endovascular Treatment Alone vs Intravenous Alteplase Plus Endovascular Treatment on Functional Independence in Patients With Acute Ischemic Stroke: The DEVT Randomized Clinical Trial
trials.population: n=234, mean 68 years; 102 women (43.6%), NIHSS proximal anterior-circulation intracranial occlusion, within 4.5 h of symptom onset and eligible for intravenous thrombolysis
trials.finding: MET the prespecified non-inferiority threshold: 63/116 (54.3%) with EVT alone vs 55/118 (46.6%) with combined treatment. The trial was STOPPED EARLY for efficacy after 234 of a planned 970 randomisations — 24% of the intended sample. The authors state the findings 'should be interpreted in the context of the clinical acceptability of the selected noninferiority threshold.'
trials.teachingPoint: A worked example of two appraisal traps at once — early stopping for efficacy and a permissive non-inferiority margin — in a trial whose headline reads as a green light to skip the lytic.

trials.name: MR CLEAN-NO IV
trials.fullName: A Randomized Trial of Intravenous Alteplase before Endovascular Treatment for Stroke
trials.population: n=539, adults, NIHSS acute ischaemic stroke eligible for both intravenous alteplase and endovascular treatment, IVT-eligible window; patients presenting directly to an EVT-capable hospital
trials.finding: DID NOT show either: median mRS 3 (IQR 2-5) with EVT alone vs 2 (IQR 2-5) with alteplase plus EVT. EVT alone was neither superior nor non-inferior — an indeterminate result on both prespecified questions.
trials.teachingPoint: Teaches that an inconclusive trial is not a licence to change practice — MR CLEAN-NO IV left the door open in both directions, which is precisely why bridging remained standard.

trials.name: SWIFT DIRECT
trials.fullName: Thrombectomy alone versus intravenous alteplase plus thrombectomy in patients with stroke: an open-label, blinded-outcome, randomised non-inferiority trial
trials.population: n=408, adults, NIHSS stroke due to large-vessel occlusion confirmed on CT or MR angiography, IVT-eligible patients admitted to endovascular centres
trials.finding: DID NOT show non-inferiority: 114/201 (57%) with thrombectomy alone vs 135/207 (65%) with alteplase plus thrombectomy. The lower limit of the one-sided 95% CI was -15.1%, crossing the -12% margin.
trials.teachingPoint: In an IVT-eligible patient already at a thrombectomy centre, omitting alteplase was not shown to be non-inferior and cost reperfusion — a concrete reason the bridging default survived.

trials.name: DIRECT-SAFE
trials.fullName: Endovascular thrombectomy versus standard bridging thrombolytic with endovascular thrombectomy within 4.5 h of stroke onset: an open-label, blinded-endpoint, randomised non-inferiority trial
trials.population: n=295, adults, NIHSS large-vessel occlusion of the intracranial internal carotid artery, MCA (M1 or M2), or basilar artery, confirmed on non-contrast CT plus vascular imaging, presented within 4.5 h of stroke onset
trials.finding: DID NOT show non-inferiority of direct thrombectomy: 80/146 (55%) direct vs 89/147 (61%) bridging. The authors conclude the study should inform guidelines to recommend bridging therapy as standard treatment.
trials.teachingPoint: A second, geographically independent trial reaching the same verdict — within 4.5 h, bridging remains the default for the IVT-eligible patient, including basilar occlusion.

trials.name: TNK-PLUS
trials.fullName: Intravenous Tenecteplase Prior to Endovascular Treatment for Ischemic Stroke at 4.5 to 24 Hours: The TNK-PLUS Randomized Clinical Trial
trials.population: n=391, median 68 years (IQR 59-75); 155 (39.6%) female, NIHSS MCA-M1 or proximal M2 occlusion, 4.5 to 24 h after last known to be well
trials.finding: DID NOT meet superiority — a null result: 88/199 (44.2%) with tenecteplase before EVT vs 83/192 (43.2%) with EVT alone. Bridging tenecteplase did not improve clinical outcomes in the 4.5-24 h window.
trials.teachingPoint: Sets the boundary on the positive early-window bridging result: beyond 4.5 h, adding tenecteplase before thrombectomy did not improve 90-day independence in a perfusion-selected proximal MCA population.

trials.name: Edinburgh CT criteria
trials.fullName: The Edinburgh CT and Genetic Diagnostic Criteria for Lobar Intracerebral Haemorrhage Associated with Cerebral Amyloid Angiopathy: Model Development and Diagnostic Test Accuracy Study
trials.population: n=110, Median 83 years (IQR 76-87); 49 (45%) men, NIHSS Not applicable — a diagnostic-accuracy study against a neuropathological reference standard, First-ever intracerebral haemorrhage diagnosed by CT; participants included between 1 June 2010 and 10 February 2016
trials.finding: Excellent discrimination, confirmed on internal bootstrap validation. Of 110 participants, ICH was lobar in 62 (56%), deep in 41 (37%) and infratentorial in 7 (6%); of the 62 lobar haemorrhages, 36 (58%) had moderate or severe CAA and 26 (42%) absent or mild CAA.
trials.teachingPoint: Gives a CT-only, and optionally CT-plus-APOE, way to grade the probability that a lobar haemorrhage is amyloid-related when MRI is unavailable — the input to how cautiously antithrombotics are restarted.

trials.name: Edinburgh criteria & ICH recurrence (IPD)
trials.fullName: Association Between the Edinburgh CT and Genetic Diagnostic Criteria for Cerebral Amyloid Angiopathy-Associated Lobar Intracerebral Haemorrhage and Recurrent Intracerebral Haemorrhage: An Individual Patient Data Meta-Analysis
trials.population: n=1705, Primary two-stage CT-only cohort (562 patients): median 76 years (IQR 68-82), 282 (50%) female, 280 (50%) male. One-stage CT-only cohort (1620): median 73 years (IQR 62-80), 763 (47%) female, 857 (53%) male. CT-APOE cohort (1006): median 71 years (IQR 58-79), 477 (47%) female, 529 (53%) male., NIHSS Not applicable — prognostic cohort analysis, Index spontaneous lobar intracerebral haemorrhage; recurrence counted only from 30 days after the index event
trials.finding: Higher Edinburgh strata were associated with more recurrent haemorrhage. In the primary two-stage CT-only analysis (562 patients from three European cohorts, 69 recurrences over 1381 person-years), 5-year recurrence occurred in 48/307 (16%) of the intermediate-and-high-risk group versus 21/255 (8%) of the low-risk group.
trials.teachingPoint: Lets a clinician grade recurrent-haemorrhage risk after a lobar ICH from the admission CT alone, when MRI-based Boston criteria are unavailable — a roughly threefold 5-year hazard between the high- and low-risk strata.

trials.name: RE-ALIGN
trials.fullName: Dabigatran versus Warfarin in Patients with Mechanical Heart Valves (RE-ALIGN)
trials.population: n=252, adults; age distribution not reported in the abstract, NIHSS not applicable - anticoagulation trial, no index stroke required for entry, two strata: mechanical valve replacement within the past 7 days, and replacement at least 3 months earlier
trials.finding: STOPPED EARLY for harm after 252 patients, because of an excess of BOTH thromboembolic and bleeding events on dabigatran. Ischemic or unspecified stroke occurred in 9 dabigatran patients (5%) and in 0 warfarin patients; major bleeding in 7 (4%) vs 2 (2%). Dose adjustment or discontinuation of dabigatran was required in 52 of 162 patients (32%) to reach the trough target
trials.teachingPoint: Teaches why a direct thrombin inhibitor is not an option for a mechanical heart valve: dabigatran produced more strokes and more bleeding than warfarin and the trial was halted for harm.

trials.name: PROACT Xa
trials.fullName: Apixaban or Warfarin in Patients with an On-X Mechanical Aortic Valve (PROACT Xa)
trials.population: n=863, adults; age distribution not reported in the abstract, NIHSS not applicable - anticoagulation trial, no index stroke required for entry, On-X aortic valve implanted at least 3 months before enrollment
trials.finding: DID NOT meet non-inferiority and DID NOT meet the OPC success criterion. The trial was STOPPED EARLY after 863 participants because of an excess of thromboembolic events on apixaban. 26 primary events occurred: 20 events in 16 apixaban participants (4.2%/patient-year) vs 6 events in 6 warfarin participants (1.3%/patient-year)
trials.teachingPoint: Teaches that no direct oral anticoagulant has been shown safe for a mechanical heart valve, including the On-X aortic valve - the one prosthesis for which the question was formally randomized, and the trial was halted for excess thromboembolism.

trials.name: BHF PROTECT-TAVI
trials.fullName: British Heart Foundation Randomised Trial of Routine Cerebral Embolic Protection during Transcatheter Aortic-Valve Implantation (BHF PROTECT-TAVI)
trials.population: n=7635, adults with aortic stenosis undergoing TAVI; mean age 81.0 years in the 3535-participant cognitive cohort, NIHSS not applicable - procedural stroke-prevention trial, randomized before TAVI; primary outcome within 72 h of the procedure or before discharge
trials.finding: NEUTRAL - routine cerebral embolic protection DID NOT reduce stroke: 81 of 3795 (2.1%) with CEP vs 82 of 3799 (2.2%) without
trials.teachingPoint: Teaches that routine filter-based cerebral embolic protection does not reduce stroke or preserve cognition at TAVI - counselling should centre on the roughly 2% procedural stroke risk itself rather than on device selection.

trials.name: PROTECTED TAVR
trials.fullName: Cerebral Embolic Protection during Transcatheter Aortic-Valve Replacement (PROTECTED TAVR)
trials.population: n=3000, adults with aortic stenosis; age distribution not reported in the abstract, NIHSS not applicable - procedural stroke-prevention trial, randomized before transfemoral TAVR; primary outcome within 72 h or before discharge
trials.finding: DID NOT show a significant effect: 2.3% with CEP vs 2.9% without. The authors state explicitly that, on the basis of the 95% confidence interval, the result may NOT rule out a benefit of CEP - this is an indeterminate trial, not a demonstrated null
trials.teachingPoint: Supplies the source of the persistent 'disabling stroke 0.5% vs 1.3%' claim for cerebral embolic protection, and the teaching that this trial could not exclude benefit while the later, larger BHF PROTECT-TAVI could.

trials.name: Warfarin resumption after ICH with a mechanical valve (meta-analysis)
trials.fullName: Resumption of Warfarin After Intracranial Hemorrhage in Patients With Mechanical Heart Valves: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
trials.population: n=788, adults; age distribution not reported in the abstract, NIHSS not applicable - intracranial hemorrhage cohort, from the index intracranial hemorrhage through the interruption and resumption period, as reported by the included studies
trials.finding: While off anticoagulation, 32 patients had an ischemic stroke - pooled event rate 5.23%, with a pooled average time to stroke of 8.08 days. After anticoagulation was resumed, 73 patients had a hemorrhagic recurrence - pooled event rate 10.95%. The authors conclude that withholding anticoagulation for up to 7 days appears relatively safe, while stating that the included studies were observational and carried SERIOUS OR CRITICAL risk of bias and that randomized trials are needed
trials.teachingPoint: Puts numbers on the mechanical-valve ICH dilemma for teaching: about 5% have an ischemic stroke while off anticoagulation, clustering around day 8, versus about 11% rebleeding after resumption - all from observational studies at serious or critical risk of bias.

trials.name: DOACs vs warfarin for LV thrombus (RCT meta-analysis)
trials.fullName: Direct oral anticoagulants or warfarin in left ventricular thrombus: an updated systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized trials
trials.population: n=554, adults; age distribution not reported in the abstract, NIHSS not applicable - anticoagulation trials in LV thrombus, not a stroke cohort, thrombus resolution assessed at 1 month and 3 months
trials.finding: NEUTRAL at both timepoints - no significant difference between DOACs and warfarin: OR 1.69 at 1 month and OR 1.39 at 3 months. The authors conclude DOACs showed comparable efficacy and safety and are a reasonable alternative to warfarin, while calling for further large-scale trials
trials.teachingPoint: Teaches that across all 7 randomized trials and 554 patients, DOACs and warfarin are statistically indistinguishable for LV thrombus - but that the intervals on stroke and bleeding are far too wide to call this proven equivalence.

trials.name: RIVAWAR
trials.fullName: Rivaroxaban vs Warfarin in Acute Left Ventricular Thrombus Following Myocardial Infarction (RIVAWAR): An Open-Label Randomised Controlled Trial
trials.population: n=261, adults; groups similar in age, sex and MI subtype, but the age range is not given in the abstract, NIHSS not applicable - LV thrombus cohort, not a stroke cohort, LV thrombus diagnosed during the index myocardial-infarction admission; treatment for 12 weeks
trials.finding: Resolution was HIGHER with rivaroxaban at 4 weeks (20% vs 8%) and EQUIVALENT at 12 weeks (95.8% vs 96.6%). By the 12-week endpoint both arms exceeded 95% resolution
trials.teachingPoint: Teaches that rivaroxaban clears post-MI LV thrombus faster than warfarin at 4 weeks but that both exceed 95% resolution by 12 weeks - and that both endpoints are imaging surrogates in a trial with no power for stroke or death.

trials.name: ARIES-HM3
trials.fullName: Aspirin and Hemocompatibility Events With a Left Ventricular Assist Device in Advanced Heart Failure: The ARIES-HM3 Randomized Clinical Trial
trials.population: n=628, adults with advanced heart failure; age range not reported in the abstract. Of the 589 analysed, 77% were men, one third were Black and 61% were White, NIHSS not applicable - device antithrombotic trial; stroke is a component of the composite, enrolled July 2020 to September 2022; median follow-up 14 months; primary endpoint at 12 months
trials.finding: Placebo (aspirin avoidance) MET non-inferiority: 74% of the placebo group vs 68% of the aspirin group were alive and free of hemocompatibility events at 12 months
trials.teachingPoint: Teaches that on a HeartMate 3 with a vitamin K antagonist, adding aspirin does not protect against stroke or pump thrombosis and increases nonsurgical bleeding - a rare instance where less antithrombotic therapy is the evidence-supported answer.

trials.name: ELSO LV venting and acute brain injury
trials.fullName: Impact of Left Ventricular Venting on Acute Brain Injury in Patients With Cardiogenic Shock: An Extracorporeal Life Support Organization Registry Analysis
trials.population: n=13276, median 58.2 years; 69.9% male, NIHSS not applicable - registry cohort of critically ill patients on mechanical circulatory support, most of whom are sedated, peripheral venoarterial ECMO runs recorded 2013-2024
trials.finding: Acute brain injury occurred in 525 of 13,276 patients (4.0%). LV-vented patients had HIGHER adjusted odds of acute brain injury (aOR 1.67) with NO difference in hospital mortality (aOR 1.07). In a propensity-matched comparison of the two venting strategies there was no difference between an intra-aortic balloon pump and a microaxial flow pump
trials.teachingPoint: Gives the base rate for neurological injury on venoarterial ECMO - about 4% of adults supported for cardiogenic shock - and flags left ventricular venting as a marker of higher neurological risk, on registry data that cannot establish cause.

trials.name: CREST
trials.fullName: Stenting versus Endarterectomy for Carotid-Artery Stenosis
trials.finding: Equivalent: 7.2% vs 6.8%
trials.teachingPoint: CAS and CEA equivalent on the composite; stroke risk favors CEA, MI risk favors CAS.

trials.name: CREST-2
trials.fullName: Medical Management and Revascularization for Asymptomatic Carotid Stenosis
trials.population: n=2485, adults, NIHSS ASYMPTOMATIC high-grade (>=70%) carotid stenosis, follow-up to 4 years
trials.finding: Stenting trial POSITIVE: 2.8% vs 6.0% medical alone. Endarterectomy trial NEUTRAL: 3.7% vs 5.3%
trials.teachingPoint: In asymptomatic >=70% stenosis on intensive medical therapy, adding stenting reduced 4-year events; adding endarterectomy did not reach significance.

trials.name: ECST-2
trials.fullName: Optimised Medical Therapy Alone versus Optimised Medical Therapy plus Revascularisation for Carotid Stenosis — 2-year interim results
trials.population: n=429, >=18, NIHSS asymptomatic or symptomatic carotid stenosis >=50% with LOW-to-INTERMEDIATE predicted risk (5-year ipsilateral stroke risk <20% by Carotid Artery Risk score), 2-year interim analysis
trials.finding: No benefit from added revascularization in this low-to-intermediate-risk group
trials.teachingPoint: For carotid stenosis with a low-to-intermediate predicted stroke risk, adding revascularization to optimised medical therapy showed no 2-year benefit.

trials.name: CADISS
trials.fullName: Cervical Artery Dissection in Stroke Study — antiplatelet treatment compared with anticoagulation treatment for cervical artery dissection
trials.population: n=250, Adults; mean age not reported in the abstract. Dissection is the commonest identified cause of ischaemic stroke in adults under 50, so the enrolled population is a young-stroke population., NIHSS Severity not reported as NIHSS. 224/250 presented with stroke or transient ischaemic attack; 26/250 presented with local symptoms only (headache, neck pain or Horner syndrome)., Symptom onset within the previous 7 days; mean time to randomisation 3.65 days (SD 1.91)
trials.finding: NO DIFFERENCE DETECTED, and the trial was far too small to detect one: stroke or death occurred in 3/126 (2%) assigned antiplatelet versus 1/124 (1%) assigned anticoagulant. Only 4 of all 250 patients (2%) had a recurrent stroke, all ipsilateral — an event rate far below what observational series had predicted.
trials.teachingPoint: Establishes that recurrent stroke after cervical artery dissection is uncommon (about 2% at 3 months) and that neither antiplatelet nor anticoagulant therapy has been shown superior — so the choice can be made on bleeding risk, adherence and cost rather than on a presumed efficacy gap.

trials.name: TREAT-CAD
trials.fullName: Aspirin versus anticoagulation in cervical artery dissection (TREAT-CAD): an open-label, randomised, non-inferiority trial
trials.population: n=194, Older than 18 years; the abstract frames cervical artery dissection as a major cause of stroke in people aged under 50, NIHSS Not reported as NIHSS; entry required symptomatic, MRI-verified cervical artery dissection, Randomised within 2 weeks of symptom onset; treatment given for 90 days
trials.finding: DID NOT meet non-inferiority. The primary endpoint occurred in 21/91 (23%) on aspirin versus 12/82 (15%) on vitamin K antagonist; the upper bound of the confidence interval (21%) exceeded the 12% non-inferiority margin, so aspirin was NOT shown to be non-inferior. Note what this does and does not say: failing to show non-inferiority is not the same as showing inferiority.
trials.teachingPoint: Aspirin was not shown to be non-inferior to a vitamin K antagonist after cervical artery dissection, and every ischaemic stroke in the trial occurred on aspirin — enough to keep anticoagulation a reasonable option in dissection, particularly where CADISS offers no reassurance to the contrary.

trials.name: CAD antithrombotic IPD meta-analysis
trials.fullName: Antithrombotic Treatment for Cervical Artery Dissection: A Systematic Review and Individual Patient Data Meta-Analysis
trials.population: n=444, Pooled participants of CADISS and TREAT-CAD; the paper opens by noting cervical artery dissection is the most common cause of stroke in younger adults, NIHSS Not reported as NIHSS in the abstract, 90 days of follow-up in both pooled trials
trials.finding: DID NOT reach statistical significance: 3/218 (1.4%) with anticoagulation versus 10/226 (4.4%) with antiplatelet therapy. The direction favours anticoagulation and the point estimate is large, but with 13 events in total the confidence interval crosses 1 and the authors' own conclusion is that no significant difference was found in preventing early recurrent events.
trials.teachingPoint: Confirms that no randomised evidence establishes either antiplatelet or anticoagulant superiority after cervical artery dissection; both remain defensible, and the decision should turn on individual bleeding risk and practical considerations rather than on a claimed efficacy difference.

trials.name: STOP-CAD
trials.fullName: Antithrombotic Treatment for Stroke Prevention in Cervical Artery Dissection: The STOP-CAD Study
trials.population: n=3636, Adults with cervical artery dissection; age distribution not given in the abstract, NIHSS Not reported as NIHSS, Outcomes assessed within 30 and 180 days of dissection
trials.finding: NO SIGNIFICANT DIFFERENCE in ischemic stroke: anticoagulation versus antiplatelet adjusted HR 0.71 (95% CI 0.45-1.12) by day 30 and 0.80 (95% CI 0.28-2.24) by day 180. Overall event rates were low — 162 new ischemic strokes (4.4%) and 28 major hemorrhages (0.8%) by day 180 — and 87.0% of all ischemic strokes had already occurred by day 30.
trials.teachingPoint: Reinforces that recurrent stroke after cervical artery dissection is front-loaded into the first 30 days, and that if anticoagulation is used it is reasonable to plan a switch to an antiplatelet before 180 days, when the bleeding excess appears.

trials.name: THEIA
trials.fullName: Thrombolysis for Central Retinal Artery Occlusion
trials.population: n=70, ≥18, NIHSS n/a, ≤4.5 h from severe vision loss
trials.finding: No significant benefit: 19/29 (66%) vs 13/27 (48%)
trials.teachingPoint: THEIA was neutral (adjusted OR 1.1, 95% CI 0.07-18.39, p=0.95; underpowered) — CRAO thrombolysis remains unproven; do not present it as evidence-supported outside trials.

trials.name: TO-ACT
trials.fullName: Endovascular Treatment With Medical Management vs Standard Care in Severe Cerebral Venous Thrombosis
trials.population: n=67, adults, NIHSS severe CVT with >=1 risk factor for poor outcome, EVT within 24 h of randomization; 12-month outcome
trials.finding: No benefit — HALTED after the first interim analysis for futility
trials.teachingPoint: Endovascular therapy for severe CVT showed no benefit and was halted for futility — anticoagulation remains first-line.

trials.name: ACTION-CVT
trials.fullName: Direct Oral Anticoagulants Versus Warfarin in the Treatment of Cerebral Venous Thrombosis
trials.population: n=845, mean 44.8; 64.7% women, NIHSS CVT on oral anticoagulation, treated Jan 2015 - Dec 2020; median follow-up 345 d
trials.finding: Similar recurrence: aHR 0.94 (95% CI 0.51-1.73); major hemorrhage LOWER with DOACs: aHR 0.35 (0.15-0.82, p=0.02)
trials.teachingPoint: DOACs perform like warfarin for CVT recurrence and recanalization with less major bleeding — a reasonable first-line option.

trials.name: CHANCE
trials.fullName: Clopidogrel with Aspirin in Acute Minor Stroke or TIA
trials.population: n=5170, ≥40, NIHSS NIHSS ≤3 (or high-risk TIA), ≤24 h
trials.finding: Favored DAPT: 8.2% vs 11.7%
trials.teachingPoint: Founding evidence for short-course DAPT in minor stroke / high-risk TIA.

trials.name: POINT
trials.fullName: Clopidogrel and Aspirin in Acute Ischemic Stroke and High-Risk TIA
trials.population: n=4881, ≥18, NIHSS NIHSS ≤3, ≤12 h
trials.finding: Favored DAPT: 5.0% vs 6.5%
trials.teachingPoint: Reinforces 21-day cap on DAPT for minor stroke.

trials.name: THALES
trials.fullName: Ticagrelor and Aspirin or Aspirin Alone in AIS or TIA
trials.population: n=11016, ≥40, NIHSS NIHSS ≤5, ≤24 h
trials.finding: Favored DAPT: 5.5% vs 6.6%
trials.teachingPoint: Supports ticagrelor-based DAPT, especially when CYP2C19 LOF suspected.

trials.name: INSPIRES
trials.fullName: Dual Antiplatelet Treatment up to 72 Hours after Ischemic Stroke
trials.population: n=6100, ≥35, NIHSS mild stroke or high-risk TIA, ≤72 h
trials.finding: Favored DAPT
trials.teachingPoint: Allows DAPT initiation up to 72 h in eligible mild stroke.

trials.name: CHANCE-2
trials.fullName: Ticagrelor or Clopidogrel with Aspirin in High-Risk TIA or Minor Stroke
trials.population: n=6412, ≥40, NIHSS NIHSS ≤3, ≤24 h
trials.finding: Favored ticagrelor: 6.0% vs 7.6%
trials.teachingPoint: Supports ticagrelor over clopidogrel in CYP2C19 LOF carriers.

trials.name: TAPIS
trials.fullName: Ticagrelor with Aspirin Dual Antiplatelet Therapy combined with Intravenous Thrombolysis in Patients with Ischaemic Stroke in China
trials.population: n=1382, Median 65.6, NIHSS 4-10, ≤6 h of onset
trials.finding: Higher with early DAPT: 68.7% vs 62.0%
trials.teachingPoint: Early oral DAPT within 6 h as an adjunct to thrombolysis improved excellent outcomes in moderate stroke — a strategy long considered contraindicated; small sICH risk not excluded.

trials.name: CMOSS
trials.fullName: Extracranial-Intracranial Bypass and Risk of Stroke and Death in Patients With Symptomatic Artery Occlusion
trials.population: n=324, median 52.7; 79.3% men, NIHSS TIA or non-disabling ischemic stroke attributed to hemodynamic insufficiency, 2 years
trials.teachingPoint: EC-IC bypass for symptomatic ICA/MCA occlusion with hemodynamic insufficiency showed no benefit over medical therapy at 2 years.

trials.name: IE baseline antithrombotic therapy and ICH
trials.fullName: Baseline Antithrombotic Therapy and Intracranial Hemorrhage Risk in Infective Endocarditis: A Multicenter Prospective Cohort Study
trials.population: n=3236, adults; age distribution not reported in the abstract, NIHSS not applicable - endocarditis cohort in which neurological events are outcomes, not entry criteria, antithrombotic exposure classified at the time of IE diagnosis; primary outcome at 30 days, mortality followed to 1 year
trials.finding: Intracranial hemorrhage occurred in 182 of 3236 patients (5.6%), with the highest incidence in the combined-therapy group (9.5%) and the anticoagulation group (6.8%). Compared with no antithrombotic therapy, baseline ANTICOAGULATION was independently associated with more ICH (adjusted risk ratio 1.83), and COMBINED therapy carried the highest risk (aRR 2.45). ANTIPLATELET therapy alone was NOT associated with ICH, and ischemic stroke rates were similar across all groups
trials.teachingPoint: Supplies the quantitative basis for teaching that anticoagulation in left-sided infective endocarditis is associated with roughly double the 30-day intracranial-hemorrhage risk without a reduction in ischemic stroke, while antiplatelet therapy alone is not - on observational data only.

trials.name: Thrombectomy for IE-related LVO (meta-analysis)
trials.fullName: Efficacy and Safety of Mechanical Thrombectomy for Patients with Infective Endocarditis-Related Large Vessel Occlusion: a Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
trials.population: n=2037, mean age 57.9 years; 62.3% women, NIHSS not reported in the abstract, acute large-vessel-occlusion stroke; individual treatment windows not reported in the pooled abstract
trials.finding: Favourable outcome (mRS 0-2) at 90 days in 29.0% of patients, with successful recanalization (mTICI 2b-3) in 76.0%. Compared with non-IE large-vessel occlusion treated with thrombectomy, IE patients had a SIGNIFICANTLY LOWER rate of favourable outcome (RR 0.48) with no significant difference in any intracranial hemorrhage (RR 1.38, 95% CI 0.96-1.98)
trials.teachingPoint: Supplies the actual numbers behind teaching on thrombectomy in endocarditis-related large-vessel occlusion - about 76% recanalization and 29% mRS 0-2, with any-ICH not significantly higher than in non-IE thrombectomy - from pooled observational series with severe heterogeneity.

trials.name: COOPER
trials.fullName: Characteristics and Outcomes of Operated Versus Nonoperated Patients With Infective Endocarditis and Cerebral Complications: the COOPER Study
trials.population: n=288, mean age 65 plus or minus 14 years; 74% male, NIHSS not reported; coma was recorded as a predictor variable, prospective enrollment 2013-2021; primary outcome at 1 month, secondary outcomes to 1 year
trials.finding: One-month all-cause mortality was significantly higher among nonoperated than operated patients: 27% vs 5.9%. On multivariable analysis, heart failure, coma and cardiac surgery were independent predictors of mortality, with surgery protective (odds ratio 0.24). Neither the type of cerebral lesion nor the timing of surgery appeared to affect prognosis
trials.teachingPoint: Provides the quantitative basis for teaching that in endocarditis with cerebral complications an indicated valve operation should be actively discussed rather than reflexively deferred, while making explicit that the 27% versus 5.9% mortality gap is confounded by indication and is an upper bound, not an effect estimate.

trials.name: IE-associated vs AF-associated stroke imaging phenotype
trials.fullName: Clinical and Imaging Characteristics of Infective Endocarditis-Associated Versus Atrial Fibrillation-Associated Stroke
trials.population: n=323, not reported in the abstract; younger age was an independent predictor of IE-associated stroke, NIHSS not reported in the abstract, acute embolic infarction at presentation; outcomes to 3 months
trials.finding: IE-associated strokes were SMALLER (21.6 plus or minus 19.3 mm vs 66.9 plus or minus 38.0 mm), more often numerous (more than 10 lesions in 44.7% vs 5.2%), and far more often involved both anterior and posterior circulations bilaterally (54.1% vs 2.6%). Independent predictors of IE-associated stroke were younger age (OR 0.87), smaller lesion size (OR 0.94) and 3-territory involvement (OR 81.21)
trials.teachingPoint: Teaches the imaging signature that should prompt blood cultures and echocardiography rather than an AF workup - numerous small infarcts spread across three vascular territories in a younger febrile patient - and sets the expectation that new ischemic lesions occur in more than half of these patients during follow-up.

trials.name: NAVIGATE ESUS
trials.fullName: Rivaroxaban for Stroke Prevention after Embolic Stroke of Undetermined Source
trials.finding: No benefit: 5.1%/yr vs 4.8%/yr
trials.teachingPoint: Rivaroxaban not superior to aspirin in ESUS and more bleeding — empiric anticoagulation not indicated.

trials.name: RE-SPECT ESUS
trials.fullName: Dabigatran for Prevention of Stroke after Embolic Stroke of Undetermined Source
trials.population: n=5390, ≥60 (or ≥45 with risk factor)
trials.finding: No benefit: 4.1%/yr vs 4.8%/yr
trials.teachingPoint: Dabigatran not superior to aspirin in ESUS — confirms NAVIGATE; no empiric DOAC.

trials.name: ARCADIA
trials.fullName: Apixaban to Prevent Recurrence after Cryptogenic Stroke in Patients with Atrial Cardiopathy
trials.finding: No benefit: 4.4%/yr vs 4.4%/yr
trials.teachingPoint: Apixaban no better than aspirin in atrial-cardiopathy ESUS — atrial cardiopathy alone does not justify anticoagulation.

trials.name: SIESTA
trials.fullName: Sedation vs Intubation for Endovascular Stroke Treatment (SIESTA)
trials.population: n=150, mean 71.5 y; 60 women (40%), NIHSS NIHSS greater than 10 required for entry; median NIHSS 17, Not specified in the abstract
trials.finding: DID NOT meet superiority: general anesthesia NIHSS 16.8 at admission to 13.6 at 24 h (difference -3.2, 95% CI -5.6 to -0.8) vs conscious sedation 17.2 to 13.6 (difference -3.6, 95% CI -5.5 to -1.7)
trials.teachingPoint: Does not support routinely avoiding general anesthesia for thrombectomy; teaches that the airway decision trades procedural stillness against hypothermia, delayed extubation and pneumonia.

trials.name: GOLIATH
trials.fullName: General or Local Anesthesia in Intra Arterial Therapy (GOLIATH)
trials.population: n=128, mean 71.4 y (SD 11.4); 62 women (48.4%), NIHSS median NIHSS 18 (IQR 14-21), Within 6 h of onset
trials.finding: DID NOT meet the prespecified hypothesis — the difference was not statistically significant, and the numerical direction favoured general anesthesia: median (IQR) growth 8.2 (2.2-38.6) mL with general anesthesia vs 19.4 (2.4-79.0) mL with conscious sedation
trials.teachingPoint: General anesthesia for thrombectomy did not produce worse tissue or clinical outcomes than conscious sedation, so an anesthesia plan should be chosen on airway, agitation and workflow grounds rather than on a presumed harm from intubation.

trials.name: AnStroke
trials.fullName: General Anesthesia Versus Conscious Sedation for Endovascular Treatment of Acute Ischemic Stroke: The AnStroke Trial (Anesthesia During Stroke)
trials.population: n=90, Not specified in the abstract, NIHSS Not specified in the abstract (admission NIHSS was recorded and balanced), Not specified in the abstract
trials.finding: NO DIFFERENCE: mRS 0-2 achieved by 19/45 (42.2%) with general anesthesia vs 18/45 (40.0%) with conscious sedation
trials.teachingPoint: Adds a neutral, physiologically controlled data point: with blood pressure managed to protocol, general anesthesia and conscious sedation produced the same 3-month outcomes.

trials.name: CANVAS II
trials.fullName: Choice of Anesthesia for Endovascular Treatment of Acute Ischemic Stroke (CANVAS II): General Anesthesia vs Conscious Sedation in Posterior Circulation Stroke
trials.population: n=87, mean 62 y (SD 12); 16 female (18.4%), 71 male (81.6%), NIHSS median NIHSS 15 (IQR 12-17), Not specified in the abstract
trials.finding: NO SIGNIFICANT DIFFERENCE: functional independence 48.8% with general anesthesia vs 54.5% with conscious sedation
trials.teachingPoint: In posterior-circulation thrombectomy, conscious sedation was not better than general anesthesia and frequently converted to it — so plan the airway ahead of the case rather than defaulting to sedation.

trials.name: GA vs non-GA Bayesian meta-analysis
trials.fullName: General Anesthesia Versus Non-GA in Endovascular Therapy for Acute Ischemic Stroke: A Systematic Review and Bayesian Meta-Analysis of RCTs
trials.population: n=1601, mean 70.0 y; 46.6% female, NIHSS Per the contributing trials, Per the contributing trials
trials.finding: Signal favouring general anesthesia, but the credible interval INCLUDES the null: OR 1.24 with a 94.2% posterior probability of superiority
trials.teachingPoint: Across all ten randomized trials, general anesthesia improves reperfusion and shows a functional-outcome signal that does not reach the level of demonstrated benefit, while costing more intraprocedural hypotension and pneumonia — a reason to stop treating conscious sedation as the safer default, not a mandate to intubate everyone.

trials.name: ATTENTION
trials.fullName: Endovascular Treatment of Acute Basilar-Artery Occlusion
trials.finding: Favored EVT: 46% vs 23%
trials.teachingPoint: Established EVT benefit for basilar-artery occlusion within 12 h.

trials.name: BAOCHE
trials.fullName: Thrombectomy 6 to 24 Hours after Stroke Due to Basilar-Artery Occlusion
trials.finding: Favored EVT: 46% vs 24%
trials.teachingPoint: Extends EVT benefit for basilar-artery occlusion to 6-24 h.

trials.name: BASICS
trials.fullName: Endovascular Therapy for Stroke Due to Basilar-Artery Occlusion
trials.population: n=300, adults, NIHSS basilar-artery occlusion, ≤6 h from estimated onset
trials.finding: NOT significant: 44.2% vs 37.7%
trials.teachingPoint: First basilar EVT RCT — neutral, but set up the severity-selected trials that later proved benefit.

trials.name: VERITAS
trials.fullName: Endovascular therapy for acute vertebrobasilar occlusion (VERITAS): a systematic review and individual patient data meta-analysis
trials.population: n=988, median 67 y (IQR 58-74); 686 (69%) male, 302 (31%) female, NIHSS Per the contributing trials; treatment effect was heterogeneous by baseline severity, with an uncertain effect at baseline NIHSS below 10, 904 of 988 patients (91%) were randomly assigned within 12 h of estimated stroke onset
trials.finding: POSITIVE: mRS 0-3 in 251/556 (45%) with endovascular therapy vs 128/432 (30%) with control
trials.teachingPoint: Pooled across all four randomized basilar trials, endovascular therapy roughly 2.4-fold increased the odds of a favourable 90-day outcome and cut 90-day mortality from 45% to 36%, at the cost of a rise in symptomatic haemorrhage from under 1% to 5%; benefit is uncertain below NIHSS 10 and greater with more proximal occlusions.

trials.name: MR CLEAN
trials.fullName: A Randomized Trial of Intraarterial Treatment for Acute Ischemic Stroke
trials.population: n=500, mean 65 (range 23-96), NIHSS moderate-severe (proximal occlusion), ≤6 h
trials.finding: Favored EVT; mRS 0-2: 32.6% vs 19.1% (absolute difference 13.5 pp, 95% CI 5.9-21.2)
trials.teachingPoint: Established EVT within 6 h for proximal anterior-circulation LVO as effective and safe on top of IV thrombolysis.

trials.name: ESCAPE
trials.fullName: Randomized Assessment of Rapid Endovascular Treatment of Ischemic Stroke
trials.population: n=316, adults, NIHSS disabling deficit (proximal occlusion), ≤12 h
trials.finding: Favored EVT; mRS 0-2: 53.0% vs 29.3% (p<0.001). Stopped early for efficacy
trials.teachingPoint: Confirmed EVT benefit with imaging-selected small core and good collaterals up to 12 h, with reduced mortality.

trials.name: EXTEND-IA
trials.fullName: Endovascular Therapy for Ischemic Stroke with Perfusion-Imaging Selection
trials.population: n=70, adults, Alteplase <4.5 h; EVT started at median 210 min
trials.finding: Both favored EVT: reperfusion median 100% vs 37% (p<0.001); early improvement 80% vs 37% (p=0.002). Stopped early for efficacy
trials.teachingPoint: Showed perfusion-selected patients gain large reperfusion and functional benefits from stent-retriever EVT added to alteplase.

trials.name: SWIFT PRIME
trials.fullName: Stent-Retriever Thrombectomy after Intravenous t-PA vs. t-PA Alone in Stroke
trials.population: n=196, adults, NIHSS moderate-severe, ≤6 h
trials.finding: Favored EVT (p<0.001); mRS 0-2: 60% vs 35% (p<0.001). Stopped early for efficacy
trials.teachingPoint: Confirmed stent-retriever EVT within 6 h on top of IV t-PA markedly increases functional independence.

trials.name: REVASCAT
trials.fullName: Thrombectomy within 8 Hours after Symptom Onset in Ischemic Stroke
trials.population: n=206, adults, NIHSS moderate-severe, ≤8 h
trials.finding: Favored EVT; mRS 0-2: 43.7% vs 28.2% (adjusted OR 2.1, 95% CI 1.1-4.0)
trials.teachingPoint: Extended the randomized EVT evidence to 8 h and to a registry-embedded, population-representative setting.

trials.name: HERMES
trials.fullName: Endovascular Thrombectomy after Large-Vessel Ischaemic Stroke: Meta-analysis of Individual Patient Data from Five Randomised Trials
trials.population: n=1287, all ages (incl. ≥80), NIHSS all enrolled, randomized ≤12 h
trials.finding: Strongly favored EVT; NNT 2.6 to reduce disability by ≥1 mRS level
trials.teachingPoint: Cemented EVT as standard of care for proximal anterior-circulation LVO, irrespective of patient characteristics.

trials.name: SELECT2
trials.fullName: Trial of Endovascular Thrombectomy for Large Ischemic Strokes
trials.finding: Favored EVT (generalized OR 1.51)
trials.teachingPoint: Supports EVT for large-core; large core is no longer an automatic exclusion.

trials.name: ANGEL-ASPECT
trials.fullName: Endovascular Therapy for Acute Ischemic Stroke with Large Infarct
trials.finding: Favored EVT
trials.teachingPoint: Confirms EVT benefit in large-core population.

trials.name: RESCUE-Japan LIMIT
trials.fullName: Endovascular Therapy for Acute Stroke with Large Ischemic Region
trials.finding: 31.0% (EVT) vs 12.7% (control)
trials.teachingPoint: First major RCT to support large-core EVT.

trials.name: TENSION
trials.fullName: Endovascular Thrombectomy for AIS with Established Large Infarct
trials.finding: Favored EVT
trials.teachingPoint: European replication of large-core EVT benefit.

trials.name: LASTE
trials.fullName: Thrombectomy for Stroke with a Large Infarct of Unrestricted Size
trials.finding: Favored EVT (median mRS 4 vs 6)
trials.teachingPoint: Thrombectomy benefits even very large infarcts (ASPECTS ≤5), at the cost of more sICH.

trials.name: ATLAS
trials.fullName: Endovascular Thrombectomy for Large-Core Ischaemic Stroke up to 24 h — Systematic Review and IPD Meta-analysis with Central Imaging Adjudication
trials.finding: Favored EVT (median mRS 4 vs 5)
trials.teachingPoint: Consolidates EVT benefit across large-core strata to 24 h, except very extensive cores (≥150 mL) beyond 6 h where evidence remains limited.

trials.name: TESLA
trials.fullName: Thrombectomy for Stroke With Large Infarct on Noncontrast CT
trials.population: n=300, median 67, NIHSS moderate-severe, ≤24 h
trials.finding: DID NOT meet superiority: UW-mRS 2.93 vs 2.27, adjusted difference 0.63 (95% CrI −0.09 to 1.34); posterior probability .96
trials.teachingPoint: Cautions that NCCT-only ASPECTS 2-5 selection up to 24 h is not clearly beneficial — context for the otherwise positive large-core class.

trials.name: DAWN
trials.fullName: Thrombectomy 6 to 24 Hours after Stroke with Mismatch between Deficit and Infarct
trials.finding: Favored EVT: 49% vs 13% (functional independence)
trials.teachingPoint: Foundational evidence for late-window EVT.

trials.name: DEFUSE-3
trials.fullName: Thrombectomy at 6-16 Hours with Selection by Perfusion Imaging
trials.finding: Favored EVT
trials.teachingPoint: Established perfusion-mismatch criteria for late-window EVT.

trials.name: MR CLEAN-LATE
trials.fullName: Endovascular Treatment 6-24 h After Stroke Selected by Collateral Flow on CT Angiography
trials.population: n=502, ≥18; 52% female, NIHSS NIHSS ≥2, 6-24 h from onset or last seen well
trials.finding: Favors EVT: median mRS 3 (IQR 2-5) vs 4 (IQR 2-6)
trials.teachingPoint: CTA collateral status alone can select late-window (6-24 h) EVT candidates who fall outside DAWN/DEFUSE-3 perfusion criteria.

trials.name: DISTAL
trials.fullName: Endovascular Treatment for Medium or Distal Vessel Occlusion Stroke — 12-Month Outcomes
trials.population: n=543, Median 77, NIHSS Median 6, ≤6 h, or 6-24 h with salvageable tissue
trials.finding: No difference (median mRS 2 vs 2)
trials.teachingPoint: No long-term benefit of EVT in mild-to-moderate medium/distal vessel occlusion — routine thrombectomy not supported in this population.

trials.name: ESCAPE-MeVO
trials.fullName: Endovascular Treatment for Medium Vessel Occlusion Stroke
trials.population: n=530, Mean 69.8, NIHSS Median 8, ≤12 h from last known well
trials.teachingPoint: Does not support routine endovascular thrombectomy for isolated medium vessel occlusion stroke outside of clinical trials.

trials.name: ORIENTAL-MeVO
trials.fullName: Endovascular Treatment of Medium-Vessel-Occlusion Strokes
trials.population: n=563, Median 71, NIHSS Median 10 (range 3-36); NIHSS >=6 required, <=24 h from onset
trials.finding: Benefit: 58.6% (280 patients) vs 46.6% (283 patients)
trials.teachingPoint: Supports considering thrombectomy for isolated medium vessel occlusion when the deficit is moderate-to-severe (NIHSS >=6), against a background of neutral trials in milder deficits. Individualize; do not read the older Class III grading as covering this population.

trials.name: DISCOUNT
trials.fullName: Mechanical Thrombectomy in Ischemic Stroke With a Medium or Distal Arterial Occlusion: The DISCOUNT Randomized Clinical Trial
trials.population: n=244, median 75 y (IQR 67-81); 56% male, NIHSS median NIHSS 8 (IQR 6-12), Within 8 h of symptom onset, or within 24 h of last seen well if no hyperintense signal was present on FLAIR imaging
trials.finding: DID NOT meet its endpoint, with the point estimate favouring medical treatment alone: 72/116 (62%) with thrombectomy vs 81/119 (68%) with medical treatment alone. The trial was STOPPED at the planned interim analysis on the recommendation of the data and safety monitoring board for futility AND an increased rate of symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage with thrombectomy.
trials.teachingPoint: Adds a randomized trial halted for futility plus a haemorrhage signal to the medium- and distal-vessel occlusion evidence, and supplies the procedural-complication data — subarachnoid haemorrhage and embolus migration — that the neutral MeVO trials do not report.

trials.name: ANGEL-REBOOT
trials.fullName: Bailout Intracranial Angioplasty or Stenting Following Thrombectomy for Acute Large-Vessel Occlusion
trials.population: n=348, median 63 (IQR 55-69); 74% male, NIHSS not restricted, ≤24 h from onset
trials.finding: Neutral, numerically worse with bailout
