trials.teachingPoint: Routine bailout angioplasty/stenting after failed or unstable thrombectomy did not improve outcome and increased dissection and hemorrhage.

trials.name: PROTECT-MT
trials.fullName: Balloon Guide Catheters for Endovascular Thrombectomy in Acute Ischaemic Stroke Due to Large-Vessel Occlusion
trials.population: n=329, median 69 (IQR 59-76); 61% male, NIHSS not restricted, ≤24 h from onset
trials.finding: WORSE with balloon guide catheter
trials.teachingPoint: Balloon guide catheters led to worse 90-day function than conventional guide catheters; the trial was halted for safety.

trials.name: ASTER
trials.fullName: Contact Aspiration vs Stent Retriever for Successful Revascularization (ASTER)
trials.population: n=381, mean 69.9 y; 174 women (45.7%), NIHSS Not specified in the abstract, Within 6 h of symptom onset; median onset-to-arterial-puncture 227 min (IQR 180-280)
trials.finding: DID NOT show a difference: 164/192 (85.4%) with contact aspiration vs 157/189 (83.1%) with stent retriever
trials.teachingPoint: Teaches that either contact aspiration or a stent retriever is a defensible first-line choice for anterior-circulation thrombectomy; the technique argument should not be presented to trainees as settled in either direction.

trials.name: COMPASS (thrombectomy)
trials.fullName: Aspiration thrombectomy versus stent retriever thrombectomy as first-line approach for large vessel occlusion (COMPASS)
trials.population: n=270, Not specified in the abstract, NIHSS Not specified in the abstract, Within 6 h of symptom onset
trials.finding: MET non-inferiority: mRS 0-2 in 69/134 (52%, 95% CI 43.8-60.3) with aspiration first pass vs 67/136 (50%, 95% CI 41.6-57.4) with stent retriever first line
trials.teachingPoint: Supports a direct-aspiration first-pass strategy as an acceptable alternative to a stent retriever for anterior-circulation thrombectomy, judged on 90-day disability rather than on angiographic reperfusion alone.

trials.name: ASTER2
trials.fullName: Thrombectomy With Combined Contact Aspiration and Stent Retriever vs Stent Retriever Alone (ASTER2)
trials.population: n=408, mean 73 y; 220 women (54%), 185 men (46%) among the 405 analysed, NIHSS Not specified in the abstract, Up to 8 h after symptom onset
trials.finding: DID NOT differ significantly: 131/203 (64.5%) combined vs 117/202 (57.9%) stent retriever alone
trials.teachingPoint: Does not support routinely combining contact aspiration with a stent retriever on the first pass; the first-pass reperfusion advantage does not survive to the end of the procedure.

trials.name: VECTOR
trials.fullName: Adaptive Endovascular Strategy to the Clot MRI in Large Intracranial Vessel Occlusion (VECTOR): stent retrievers plus contact aspiration versus contact aspiration alone in susceptibility-vessel-sign-positive stroke
trials.population: n=521, median 74.9 y (IQR 64.4-83.3); 284 (55%) female, 237 (45%) male, NIHSS Not specified in the abstract, Arterial puncture within 24 h of symptom onset
trials.finding: DID NOT differ significantly: 152/263 (58%) combined vs 135/258 (52%) contact aspiration alone
trials.teachingPoint: Even when the clot is selected on MRI as red-cell-rich, adding a stent retriever to contact aspiration on the first pass does not improve near-complete reperfusion within three passes; either first-line strategy remains defensible.

trials.name: EXTEND
trials.fullName: Thrombolysis Guided by Perfusion Imaging up to 9 Hours after Onset
trials.population: n=225, 18-80, NIHSS 4-26, 4.5-9 h or wake-up
trials.finding: Favored alteplase: 35.4% vs 29.5%
trials.teachingPoint: Supports perfusion-mismatch IVT in 4.5-9 h window when EVT not indicated.

trials.name: EPITHET
trials.fullName: Echoplanar Imaging Thrombolytic Evaluation Trial
trials.finding: Primary endpoint not met: infarct growth non-significantly lower with alteplase; reperfusion significantly more common
trials.teachingPoint: Conceptual basis for later mismatch-based late-window trials.

trials.name: ECASS4-EXTEND
trials.fullName: Extending the Time Window for IV Thrombolysis Using MRI-based Selection
trials.finding: Favored alteplase numerically; not statistically significant after early termination
trials.teachingPoint: Adds to the late-window mismatch evidence base; not independently practice-changing.

trials.name: TIMELESS
trials.fullName: Tenecteplase for Stroke at 4.5 to 24 Hours with Perfusion-Imaging Selection
trials.finding: Favored TNK numerically; primary endpoint did not reach significance overall
trials.teachingPoint: Cautionary: late-window TNK alone (with EVT permitted) did not meet its primary endpoint.

trials.name: TRACE-III
trials.fullName: Tenecteplase for Ischemic Stroke 4.5-24 Hours without Thrombectomy
trials.finding: Favored TNK: 33.0% vs 24.2%
trials.teachingPoint: Strongest evidence to date for late-window TNK in EVT-ineligible LVO.

trials.name: HOPE
trials.fullName: Alteplase for Acute Ischemic Stroke at 4.5 to 24 Hours: The HOPE Randomized Clinical Trial
trials.finding: Favored alteplase: 40% vs 26%
trials.teachingPoint: Adds positive evidence for perfusion-selected late-window IV thrombolysis in EVT-ineligible patients; remains selective and consult-dependent, not routine.

trials.name: EXPECTS
trials.fullName: Alteplase for Posterior Circulation Ischemic Stroke at 4.5 to 24 Hours
trials.population: n=234, adults, NIHSS median 3 (mainly mild), 4.5-24 h
trials.finding: Favored alteplase: 89.6% vs 72.6%
trials.teachingPoint: Supports late-window thrombolysis for selected mild posterior-circulation stroke without perfusion mismatch requirement; remains emerging, not routine.

trials.name: CHABLIS-T II
trials.fullName: Tenecteplase Thrombolysis for Stroke up to 24 Hours After Onset With Perfusion Imaging Selection (CHABLIS-T II)
trials.population: n=224, adults, 4.5-24 h
trials.finding: 33.3% (37/111) vs 10.8% (12/113); no significant difference in 90-day clinical outcomes
trials.teachingPoint: Adds to the mixed late-window TNK evidence base; reinforces that reperfusion gains have not consistently translated to clinical benefit.

trials.name: OCEANIC-STROKE
trials.fullName: Asundexian for Secondary Stroke Prevention
trials.finding: Lower with asundexian: 6.2% vs 8.4%
trials.teachingPoint: Asundexian on top of antiplatelets cut ischaemic stroke ~26% without more major bleeding — could reshape noncardioembolic prevention.

trials.name: OCEANIC-AF
trials.fullName: Asundexian versus Apixaban in Patients with Atrial Fibrillation
trials.population: n=14810, mean 73.9 ± 7.7; 35.2% women, NIHSS mean CHA₂DS₂-VASc 4.3 ± 1.3; 18.2% prior stroke or TIA, stopped prematurely on DMC recommendation
trials.finding: Asundexian markedly WORSE: 1.3% (98 patients) vs 0.4% (26 patients)
trials.teachingPoint: Asundexian is inferior to apixaban for AF stroke prevention (HR 3.79) despite less bleeding — do not substitute it for a DOAC.

trials.name: AXIOMATIC-SSP
trials.fullName: Safety and Efficacy of Factor XIa Inhibition with Milvexian for Secondary Stroke Prevention
trials.population: n=2366, adults, NIHSS acute ischaemic stroke or high-risk TIA, 90-day treatment period
trials.finding: NEUTRAL: placebo 16.8% vs milvexian arms 15.3-16.7%; no significant dose-response
trials.teachingPoint: Milvexian added to DAPT showed no efficacy signal but also no bleeding excess — groundwork for phase 3.

trials.name: SOUL
trials.fullName: Oral Semaglutide and Cardiovascular Outcomes in High-Risk Type 2 Diabetes (SOUL)
trials.population: n=9650, 50 years or older, NIHSS not applicable — enrolment by vascular and renal risk, not stroke severity, mean follow-up 47.5 ± 10.9 months; median 49.5 months
trials.finding: MET superiority: 579 of 4825 (12.0%; 3.1 events per 100 person-years) with oral semaglutide vs 668 of 4825 (13.8%; 3.7 per 100 person-years) with placebo
trials.teachingPoint: Establishes that an oral GLP-1 receptor agonist reduces major adverse cardiovascular events in high-risk type 2 diabetes, giving a tablet option for vascular risk reduction where injection is a barrier.

trials.name: SURPASS-CVOT
trials.fullName: Cardiovascular Outcomes with Tirzepatide versus Dulaglutide in Type 2 Diabetes (SURPASS-CVOT)
trials.population: n=13165, mean 64.1 ± 8.8 years; 29.0% women, NIHSS not applicable — enrolment by diabetes and atherosclerotic disease status, event-driven; follow-up duration not stated in the abstract
trials.finding: MET non-inferiority but DID NOT meet superiority: 801 events (12.2%) with tirzepatide vs 862 (13.1%) with dulaglutide
trials.teachingPoint: Caps expectations for incretin therapy: tirzepatide matched but did not beat dulaglutide on cardiovascular events, so agent choice within the class should turn on glycemic, weight, tolerability and access considerations rather than on an assumed cardiovascular advantage.

trials.name: Danish Hormonal Contraception Cohort
trials.fullName: Stroke and myocardial infarction with contemporary hormonal contraception: real-world, nationwide, prospective cohort study
trials.population: n=2025691, Women aged 15-49 years, NIHSS Not applicable — incident first-ever events ascertained from national registry discharge diagnoses, not a severity-stratified cohort, Denmark, 1996 to 2021; 22,209,697 person-years of follow-up
trials.finding: POSITIVE ASSOCIATION for every systemic route except the levonorgestrel IUD. 4730 ischaemic strokes and 2072 myocardial infarctions occurred. Standardised ischaemic stroke rate per 100,000 person-years: 18 (95% CI 18 to 19) no use, 39 (36 to 42) combined oral contraception, 33 (25 to 44) progestin-only pills, 23 (17 to 29) intrauterine device. Combined oral contraception carried an adjusted rate ratio of 2.0 (1.9 to 2.2) for ischaemic stroke, equating to 21 (18 to 24) extra strokes per 100,000 person-years — a doubling of a small number.
trials.teachingPoint: Gives numbers for the contraception conversation: systemic hormonal methods roughly double a small absolute arterial risk in women aged 15-49, while the levonorgestrel intrauterine device shows no detected increase — making it the default option to discuss when arterial risk is the deciding factor.

trials.name: Danish Progestogen-Only Contraceptive Cohort
trials.fullName: Risk of ischemic and hemorrhagic stroke in users of progestogen-only contraceptives: A Danish registry study
trials.population: n=1734905, Non-pregnant women aged 18-49 years, NIHSS Not applicable — registry-ascertained incident stroke events, Denmark, 2004 to 2021; 16,854,953 person-years of follow-up
trials.finding: NULL against non-use: compared with non-use of hormonal contraception, NO progestogen-only method was associated with an increased adjusted incidence rate ratio for either ischemic stroke or intracerebral haemorrhage. Against combined hormonal contraceptives containing ethinylestradiol, ischemic stroke rates were roughly halved: desogestrel-only pills IRR 0.56 and levonorgestrel IUD IRR 0.44.
trials.teachingPoint: Supports progestogen-only contraceptives — pills, implants, injections and the levonorgestrel IUD — as reasonable alternatives when stroke risk is a deciding factor, while making clear that the absolute gain from switching is small.

trials.name: CHOICE
trials.fullName: Intra-arterial Alteplase Following Successful Thrombectomy
trials.population: n=121, ≥18, NIHSS all, post-EVT
trials.finding: Favored alteplase: 59.0% vs 40.4%
trials.teachingPoint: IA alteplase after successful EVT may improve outcomes; not yet standard of care.

trials.name: CHOICE-2
trials.fullName: Adjunctive Intra-Arterial Alteplase After Successful Thrombectomy for Acute Ischemic Stroke
trials.population: n=440, Median 76, ≤24 h
trials.finding: Higher with IA alteplase: 57.5% vs 42.5%
trials.teachingPoint: IA alteplase after successful EVT improved excellent outcomes and reperfusion — but a higher mortality signal warrants caution before adoption.

trials.name: PEARL
trials.fullName: Intra-Arterial Alteplase After Successful Endovascular Reperfusion in Acute Stroke
trials.population: n=324, median 68 y (IQR 58-75), NIHSS not restricted by protocol NIHSS band (anterior-circulation LVO), ≤24 h from symptom onset to thrombectomy
trials.finding: MET superiority, favoring IA alteplase: 44.8% (73/163) vs 30.2% (48/159)
trials.teachingPoint: Strengthens, but does not settle, the case for adjunctive IA alteplase 0.225 mg/kg after successful anterior-circulation thrombectomy; the accompanying numerically higher mortality means it remains an unadopted, guideline-unclassed adjunct rather than a standard step.

trials.name: ANGEL-TNK
trials.fullName: Intra-arterial Tenecteplase for Acute Stroke After Successful Endovascular Therapy
trials.population: n=256, median 71.6 y (IQR 61.3-79.2); 44.1% female, NIHSS not restricted by a protocol NIHSS band (anterior-circulation LVO), 4.5 to 24 h from last known well
trials.finding: MET superiority, favoring IA tenecteplase: 40.5% (51/126) vs 26.4% (34/129)
trials.teachingPoint: Extends the adjunctive-lysis hypothesis to intra-arterial tenecteplase in the late window, but a positive primary with no supporting secondary endpoint is not a basis to adopt it; it remains investigational with no guideline class.

trials.name: IAT-TOP
trials.fullName: Intra-arterial Alteplase Thrombolysis After Successful Thrombectomy for Acute Ischemic Stroke in the Posterior Circulation
trials.population: n=246, median 65.0 y (IQR 56.0-72.0); 176 male (71.5%), NIHSS not restricted by a protocol NIHSS band (acute basilar artery occlusion), ≤24 h from time last known well
trials.finding: DID NOT meet superiority — flatly neutral and numerically favoring control: 41.9% (52/124) with IA alteplase vs 46.7% (57/122) control
trials.teachingPoint: Argues against extrapolating adjunctive intra-arterial alteplase from the anterior circulation to basilar occlusion — after successful basilar recanalization it was safe but produced no functional gain.

trials.name: IA Tenecteplase Dose-Escalation Trial
trials.fullName: Intra-Arterial Tenecteplase After Successful Reperfusion in Large Vessel Occlusion Stroke: A Phase 1b/2a Dose-Escalation and Dose-Expansion Randomized Clinical Trial
trials.population: n=205, median 71 y (IQR 60-77); 113 (55.1%) male, NIHSS not restricted by a protocol NIHSS band (anterior-circulation LVO), ≤24 h from last known well
trials.finding: Phase 1b: the 0.1250 mg/kg tier CROSSED the prespecified safety threshold (sICH in 3 of 12 patients, P=.04); sICH occurred in 1 of 14 at 0.0313 mg/kg and 2 of 22 at 0.0625 mg/kg. Phase 2a DID NOT demonstrate benefit at either surviving dose: mRS 0-1 33.8% (22/65) control vs 37.0% (17/46) at 0.0313 mg/kg vs 43.5% (20/46) at 0.0625 mg/kg
trials.teachingPoint: Shows that the safety of adjunctive intra-arterial tenecteplase is dose-dependent and that the 0.125 mg/kg tier tripped a prespecified hemorrhage boundary in escalation — dose, not just drug class, has to be specified before any adjunctive-lysis claim is made.

trials.name: IA Thrombolysis Dose Network Meta-analysis
trials.fullName: Dose-Specific Intra-Arterial Thrombolysis After Endovascular Thrombectomy for Large-Vessel Occlusion Stroke: A Network Meta-Analysis of Randomized Trials
trials.population: n=2126, median approximately 69 y; approximately 40% women, NIHSS as per the seven contributing randomized trials, as per the contributing trials (angiographic reperfusion achieved after EVT)
trials.finding: Signal confined to two regimens: IA alteplase 0.225 mg/kg OR 1.94 vs control, and tenecteplase 0.125 mg/kg OR 1.90 vs control; lower-dose tenecteplase (0.0625 and 0.03125 mg/kg) and urokinase showed attenuated or uncertain effects
trials.teachingPoint: Frames adjunctive intra-arterial lysis as a dose-specific question rather than a settled class effect, and explicitly does not support adopting any regimen into practice on current evidence.

trials.name: CASSISS
trials.fullName: Stenting Plus Medical Therapy vs Medical Therapy Alone for Symptomatic Severe Intracranial Atherosclerotic Stenosis
trials.population: n=358, mean 56.3; 73.5% male, NIHSS TIA or non-disabling, non-perforator-territory stroke, enrolled beyond 3 weeks from the latest ischemic event; followed 3 years
trials.finding: No significant difference between stenting and medical therapy
trials.teachingPoint: Intracranial stenting added no benefit over medical therapy for symptomatic 70-99% stenosis, even with refined selection and experienced operators.

trials.name: SAMMPRIS
trials.fullName: Stenting versus Aggressive Medical Therapy for Intracranial Arterial Stenosis
trials.population: n=451, adults, NIHSS recent TIA or stroke, recent qualifying event
trials.finding: HARM from stenting: 30-day stroke/death 14.7% vs 5.8% (P=0.002); 1-year primary endpoint 20.0% vs 12.2%. Enrolment stopped early
trials.teachingPoint: Aggressive medical management — not stenting — is first-line for symptomatic 70-99% intracranial stenosis.

trials.name: ANNEXA-I
trials.fullName: Andexanet for Factor Xa Inhibitor-Associated Acute ICH
trials.population: n=530, ≥18, NIHSS n/a, ≤15 h from last FXa dose, ≤6 h from ICH onset
trials.finding: Favored andexanet: 67.0% vs 53.1%
trials.teachingPoint: AHA/ASA 2022 lists andexanet as Class IIa for FXa-associated ICH; ANNEXA-I refines hemostatic-vs-thrombotic trade-off.

trials.name: ANNEXA-4
trials.fullName: Full Study Report of Andexanet Alfa for Bleeding Associated with Factor Xa Inhibitors
trials.population: n=352, mean 77, NIHSS acute major bleeding, ≤18 h after factor Xa inhibitor dose
trials.finding: Anti-Xa activity reduced 92% (apixaban and rivaroxaban); excellent/good hemostasis 82% (204/249)
trials.teachingPoint: Established andexanet reverses anti-Xa activity with 82% good hemostasis, at a 10% 30-day thrombotic event rate.

trials.name: Andexanet vs 4F-PCC meta-analysis
trials.fullName: Efficacy and Safety of Andexanet Alfa Versus Four Factor Prothrombin Complex Concentrate for Emergent Reversal of Factor Xa Inhibitor Associated Intracranial Hemorrhage: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
trials.population: n=2977, Not reported in aggregate across the 16 included studies, NIHSS Not reported, Emergent reversal on presentation, as defined by each source study; literature searched to 16 May 2024
trials.finding: Mixed, and internally inconsistent. Haemostatic efficacy favoured andexanet (RR 1.10). Overall mortality was lower with andexanet (RR 0.67), yet 30-day mortality specifically DID NOT differ (RR 0.82). Thromboembolic events were MORE frequent with andexanet (RR 1.47).
trials.teachingPoint: Teaches that no randomised trial has ever compared andexanet with 4F-PCC head to head, and that US practice reverted to 4F-PCC because andexanet was withdrawn from the US market in December 2025 — a regulatory and supply consequence, not a demonstration that 4F-PCC works better.

trials.name: INTERACT3
trials.fullName: Care Bundle Approach for Acute Intracerebral Haemorrhage
trials.population: n=7036, ≥18, NIHSS n/a, <6 h from onset
trials.finding: Favored bundle
trials.teachingPoint: Establishes care-bundle approach for acute ICH.

trials.name: INTERACT2
trials.fullName: Rapid Blood-Pressure Lowering in Acute Intracerebral Hemorrhage
trials.finding: Negative primary: 52.0% vs 55.6%
trials.teachingPoint: Supports early BP reduction in ICH; ordinal benefit despite a negative dichotomous primary.

trials.name: ATACH-2
trials.fullName: Intensive Blood-Pressure Lowering in Acute Cerebral Hemorrhage
trials.finding: No benefit: 38.7% vs 37.7%
trials.teachingPoint: More intensive target (<140) gave no benefit and more renal AEs — avoid overshoot below ~140.

trials.name: INTERACT1-4 pooled
trials.fullName: Effects of Blood Pressure Lowering in Relation to Time in Acute Intracerebral Haemorrhage: A Pooled Analysis of the Four INTERACT Trials
trials.population: n=11312, Mean 63 years (SD 12.7); 4066 (35.9%) female, 7246 (64.1%) male, NIHSS Not used; baseline severity handled through the ICH score in the heterogeneity analyses, Median 2.9 h from symptom onset to randomisation (IQR 1.8-4.1); INTERACT1-3 enrolled within 6 h of onset, INTERACT4 within 2 h
trials.finding: Favoured intensive BP lowering: significantly decreased odds of poor physical function (mRS 3-6)
trials.teachingPoint: Supports starting BP lowering as early as possible after ICH — ideally within about 3 hours of onset — while making explicit that the benefit is not mediated by reduced haematoma growth.

trials.name: Deep vs lobar ICH BP meta-analysis
trials.fullName: Functional Outcomes After Intensive Blood Pressure Reduction in Deep and Lobar Intracerebral Hemorrhage
trials.population: n=9022, Mean 63 years; 37% female (both analysis steps), NIHSS Not used; ATACH-2 individual patient data were adjusted for Glasgow Coma Scale score and presence of intraventricular haemorrhage, Acute ICH windows as defined by the three parent trials; the analysis did not stratify by time from onset
trials.finding: DID NOT demonstrate a significant benefit of intensive BP reduction in either location. Step 1: deep OR 0.89, lobar OR 0.92. Step 2 (with INTERACT3 added): deep OR 0.82, lobar OR 0.97. All four confidence intervals cross 1.00.
trials.teachingPoint: Teaches that the deep-versus-lobar question in acute BP management is unresolved: current evidence neither establishes a location-specific benefit nor rules one out, so location should not by itself change the acute BP target.

trials.name: TICH-2
trials.fullName: Tranexamic Acid for Hyperacute Primary Intracerebral Haemorrhage
trials.population: n=2325, adults, NIHSS not restricted, ≤8 h from onset
trials.finding: Neutral: no significant shift
trials.teachingPoint: Tranexamic acid is not routine in spontaneous ICH — no functional benefit, though it is safe and reduces early death.

trials.name: FASTEST
trials.fullName: Recombinant Factor VIIa versus Placebo for Spontaneous Intracerebral Haemorrhage within 2 h of Symptom Onset
trials.population: n=626, adults, NIHSS spontaneous ICH, ≤2 h from onset (mean 100 min)
trials.finding: NEGATIVE: adjusted common OR 1.09; trial met prespecified futility criteria at 2nd interim analysis
trials.teachingPoint: rFVIIa has no role in spontaneous ICH even at ≤2 h: no functional benefit, more thrombotic harm.

trials.name: STOP-MSU
trials.fullName: Tranexamic Acid Versus Placebo in Individuals with Intracerebral Haemorrhage Treated Within 2 h of Symptom Onset (STOP-MSU)
trials.population: n=201, Median 66 years (IQR 55-77); 82 (41%) female, 119 (59%) male, NIHSS Not reported in the primary publication, Investigational product commenced within 2 h of symptom onset
trials.finding: DID NOT reduce haematoma growth, and the point estimate favoured placebo: growth occurred in 43/101 (43%) assessable participants given tranexamic acid versus 37/97 (38%) given placebo
trials.teachingPoint: Do not give tranexamic acid for primary ICH outside a trial — treating within 2 hours of onset still did not slow the bleed.

trials.name: TRIDENT
trials.fullName: Three Low-Dose Antihypertensive Agents in a Single Pill after Intracerebral Hemorrhage
trials.finding: Lower with triple pill: 4.6% vs 7.4%
trials.teachingPoint: A simplified low-dose triple pill after ICH lowers recurrent stroke and CV events — supports intensive, simplified BP-lowering.

trials.name: RESTART
trials.fullName: REstart or STop Antithrombotics Randomised Trial — antiplatelet therapy after intracerebral haemorrhage
trials.population: n=537, ≥18, NIHSS ICH survivors, randomized a median of 76 days (IQR 29-146) after ICH; followed up to 5 years
trials.finding: Fewer recurrences with antiplatelet therapy: 4% (12/268) vs 9% (23/268)
trials.teachingPoint: Restarting antiplatelet therapy after ICH did not raise recurrent hemorrhage; the risk is likely outweighed by secondary-prevention benefit.

trials.name: PEACH
trials.fullName: Safety and Efficacy of Prophylactic Levetiracetam for Prevention of Epileptic Seizures in the Acute Phase of Intracerebral Haemorrhage (PEACH)
trials.population: n=50, Aged 18 years or older, NIHSS Randomisation stratified by baseline NIHSS; the enrolled cohort is described as mild-to-moderate severity intracerebral haemorrhage, Randomised within 24 h of onset; continuous EEG started within 24 h of inclusion and recorded over 48 h
trials.finding: Favoured levetiracetam: a clinical or electrographic seizure occurred in 3/19 (16%) on levetiracetam versus 10/23 (43%) on placebo. Every seizure captured in the first 72 h was electrographic only — none were clinical.
trials.teachingPoint: Teaches why prophylactic levetiracetam after ICH remains a research question rather than routine care: PEACH reduced EEG-detected seizures in 42 analysable patients and says nothing about function, so guidelines still advise against routine prophylaxis.

trials.name: ENRICH
trials.fullName: Early Minimally Invasive Removal of Intracerebral Hemorrhage
trials.population: n=300, 18-80, NIHSS n/a, ≤24 h from onset
trials.finding: Favored surgery (Bayesian posterior probability >0.95)
trials.teachingPoint: Supports early minimally invasive evacuation for lobar ICH at capable centers.

trials.name: MISTIE III
trials.fullName: Minimally Invasive Surgery with Thrombolysis in ICH Evacuation
trials.finding: Negative: 45% vs 41%
trials.teachingPoint: No overall functional benefit; safe; outcome depends on achieving adequate evacuation.

trials.name: MIND
trials.fullName: Minimally Invasive Surgery vs Medical Management Alone for Intracerebral Hemorrhage: The MIND Randomized Clinical Trial
trials.population: n=236, 18-80, NIHSS ≥6, ≤72 h (surgery)
trials.finding: No significant benefit of surgery
trials.teachingPoint: Tempers enthusiasm for minimally invasive ICH evacuation; MIS benefit appears pathway- and technique-specific (cf. ENRICH), not universal.

trials.name: SWITCH
trials.fullName: Decompressive Craniectomy plus Best Medical Treatment vs Best Medical Treatment Alone for Severe Deep ICH
trials.population: n=201, 18-75, NIHSS n/a, Severe deep (basal ganglia/thalamic) spontaneous ICH
trials.finding: Favoured surgery numerically but not significant: 44% vs 58%
trials.teachingPoint: Objective: numerically fewer very-poor outcomes with craniectomy, but not statistically significant; no safety excess.

trials.name: STICH
trials.fullName: International Surgical Trial in Intracerebral Haemorrhage — early surgery vs initial conservative treatment
trials.population: n=1033, adults, NIHSS clinical-status stratified (good vs poor prognosis), surgery within 24 h of randomization
trials.finding: Neutral: 26% vs 24% favourable
trials.teachingPoint: No overall benefit from routine early craniotomy for supratentorial ICH — the basis for medical management as default in equipoise.

trials.name: STICH II
trials.fullName: Early surgery versus initial conservative treatment in spontaneous supratentorial lobar intracerebral haematomas
trials.population: n=601, adults, NIHSS conscious patients, ≤48 h from ictus; surgery within 12 h of randomization
trials.finding: Neutral: unfavourable in 59% vs 62%
trials.teachingPoint: Early open surgery for superficial lobar ICH without IVH is not beneficial; motivates minimally invasive approaches instead.

trials.name: Hyponatremia & ICH
trials.fullName: Severity-Stratified Hyponatremia Is Associated with Increased Mortality and Complications in Nontraumatic Intracerebral Hemorrhage
trials.population: n=45114, Serum Na ≤7 d of diagnosis
trials.finding: Moderate 17.5% vs 13.3%; severe 18.7% vs 12.9%
trials.teachingPoint: Serum sodium is a readily-available risk-stratification marker in acute ICH; supports vigilant Na monitoring (causality not established).

trials.name: CONVINCE
trials.fullName: Long-Term Colchicine for the Prevention of Vascular Recurrent Events in Non-Cardioembolic Stroke
trials.population: n=3144, adults, NIHSS non-severe ischemic stroke or high-risk TIA, long-term; randomized 2016-2022, follow-up to Jan 2024
trials.finding: Neutral: 9.8% vs 11.7% (3.32 vs 3.92 per 100 person-years)
trials.teachingPoint: Colchicine is not established for stroke prevention — CONVINCE was neutral but underpowered; read with CHANCE-3.

trials.name: CHANCE-3
trials.fullName: Colchicine in Patients with Acute Ischaemic Stroke or Transient Ischaemic Attack
trials.population: n=8343, ≥40, NIHSS minor-to-moderate ischemic stroke or TIA, randomized within 24 h of onset; treated 90 days
trials.finding: Neutral: 6.3% vs 6.5%
trials.teachingPoint: Ninety days of colchicine after minor stroke/TIA with raised hs-CRP did not reduce recurrent stroke.

trials.name: CLEAR SYNERGY (colchicine)
trials.fullName: Colchicine in Acute Myocardial Infarction (CLEAR SYNERGY / OASIS-9)
trials.population: n=7062, adults, NIHSS acute myocardial infarction, median follow-up 3 years
trials.finding: Neutral: 9.1% vs 9.3%
trials.teachingPoint: Colchicine after MI did not reduce cardiovascular events despite lowering CRP — consistent with the neutral stroke trials.

trials.name: Anti-inflammatory CV meta-analysis
trials.fullName: Effects of anti-inflammatory agents on cardiovascular outcomes: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials
trials.population: n=82208, not reported in the abstract — trial-level meta-analysis, NIHSS not applicable, Medline, Embase and Cochrane searched from inception to 8 October 2024; trials required at least 100 patient-years of follow-up per treatment arm
trials.finding: The effect on MACE VARIED BY DRUG CLASS rather than being uniform — driven by colchicine (RR 0.76, moderate certainty) and canakinumab (RR 0.88, moderate certainty), with NO benefit observed for other agents
trials.teachingPoint: Reframes anti-inflammatory vascular prevention as class- and population-specific rather than general, and supplies the reason the neutral cerebrovascular colchicine trials should be taken at face value rather than explained away.

trials.name: CLEAR III
trials.fullName: Thrombolytic Removal of Intraventricular Haemorrhage in Treatment of Severe Stroke
trials.population: n=500, adults, NIHSS not restricted, ICU, after EVD placement
trials.finding: Neutral: 48% vs 45%
trials.teachingPoint: EVD alteplase for obstructive IVH reduces mortality but does not improve functional outcome and increases survival at mRS 5.

trials.name: LAAOS III
trials.fullName: Left Atrial Appendage Occlusion during Cardiac Surgery to Prevent Stroke
trials.population: n=4770, mean 71, NIHSS AF with mean CHA₂DS₂-VASc 4.2 (≥2 required), mean follow-up 3.8 years
trials.finding: Favors occlusion: 4.8% vs 7.0%
trials.teachingPoint: Concomitant surgical LAA occlusion during cardiac surgery reduced stroke/systemic embolism by a third, additive to ongoing anticoagulation.

trials.name: OPTION
trials.fullName: Left Atrial Appendage Closure after Ablation for Atrial Fibrillation
trials.population: n=1600, mean 69.6 ± 7.7; 34.1% women, NIHSS CHA₂DS₂-VASc ≥2 in men, ≥3 in women (mean 3.5 ± 1.3), 36 months
trials.finding: Safety superior — 8.5% vs 18.1%; efficacy non-inferior — 5.3% vs 5.8%
trials.teachingPoint: After AF ablation, LAA closure was non-inferior to anticoagulation for death/stroke/embolism with about half the non-procedural bleeding.

trials.name: SPS3
trials.fullName: Secondary Prevention of Small Subcortical Strokes — clopidogrel added to aspirin after lacunar stroke
trials.population: n=3020, mean 63; 63% men, NIHSS recent symptomatic lacunar infarct, long-term secondary prevention; mean follow-up 3.4 years
trials.finding: Neutral: 2.5%/y (DAPT) vs 2.7%/y (aspirin)
trials.teachingPoint: Do not use long-term aspirin + clopidogrel after lacunar stroke — no benefit, doubled major bleeding, increased mortality.

trials.name: SSI antiplatelet network meta-analysis
trials.fullName: Efficacy and safety of antiplatelet therapy for secondary prevention of small subcortical infarction: a systematic review and network meta-analysis
trials.population: n=47507, not reported in the abstract — trial-level network meta-analysis, NIHSS not reported; enrolment was by small subcortical infarction subtype, Medline, Embase, Cochrane Library and Web of Science searched from inception to October 2024; PROSPERO CRD42024607819
trials.finding: Cilostazol ranked best for preventing MACE (SUCRA 90.0%), significantly better than aspirin, dipyridamole, vorapaxar, sarpogrelate and placebo; the comparison with ticlopidine touches unity and is NOT significant
trials.teachingPoint: Reinforces avoiding long-term aspirin plus clopidogrel after small subcortical infarction on bleeding grounds, and flags cilostazol as the best-ranked single agent in a largely East Asian evidence base that has not been replicated in Western populations.

trials.name: VESALIUS-CV
trials.fullName: Evolocumab in Patients without a Previous Myocardial Infarction or Stroke (VESALIUS-CV)
trials.population: n=12257, median 66 years; 43% women, 93% White, NIHSS not applicable — no prior stroke permitted, median follow-up 4.6 years
trials.finding: MET both primary end points. 3-point MACE in 336 patients (5-year KM 6.2%) with evolocumab vs 443 (8.0%) with placebo; 4-point MACE in 747 (13.4%) vs 907 (16.2%)
trials.teachingPoint: Teaches that the PCSK9 evidence base now reaches patients with atherosclerosis or diabetes and no prior event — but explicitly not stroke survivors, for whom SPARCL and Treat Stroke to Target remain the anchors.

trials.name: Ez-PAVE
trials.fullName: Intensive LDL Cholesterol Targeting in Atherosclerotic Cardiovascular Disease (Ez-PAVE)
trials.population: n=3048, 19-80 years by protocol; age distribution not reported in the abstract, NIHSS not reported — enrolment was by ASCVD status, not stroke severity, median follow-up 3.0 years
trials.finding: MET superiority: 100 events (Kaplan-Meier cumulative incidence 6.6%) with the <55 mg/dL target vs 147 events (9.7%) with the <70 mg/dL target
trials.teachingPoint: Adds randomized support for pushing LDL below 55 mg/dL in established atherosclerotic disease, while teaching why an open-label composite containing 'any revascularization' cannot be read as a stroke-specific result.

trials.name: CHARM
trials.fullName: Intravenous Glibenclamide for Cerebral Oedema after Large Hemispheric Stroke
trials.population: n=535, 18-85 (primary analysis restricted to 18-70), NIHSS large hemispheric infarction, study drug started within 10 h of onset
trials.finding: Trial STOPPED EARLY for slow COVID-era enrolment before the planned sample was reached
trials.teachingPoint: IV glibenclamide for large hemispheric infarction remains unproven — CHARM was halted early and underpowered.

trials.name: DECIMAL
trials.fullName: Early Decompressive Craniectomy in Malignant Middle Cerebral Artery Infarction
trials.population: n=38, 18-55, NIHSS malignant MCA infarction, early (protocol ≤24 h of randomization eligibility)
trials.finding: mRS ≤3: 25% vs 5.6% at 6 mo (P=0.18); 50% vs 22.2% at 1 y (P=0.10) — underpowered; mortality reduced by 52.8 pp (P<0.0001)
trials.teachingPoint: One of the three European trials whose pooled analysis made early hemicraniectomy standard for malignant MCA infarction in younger patients.

trials.name: DESTINY
trials.fullName: Decompressive Surgery for the Treatment of Malignant Infarction of the Middle Cerebral Artery
trials.population: n=32, adults (≤60 by design), NIHSS malignant MCA infarction, early hemicraniectomy
trials.finding: 30-day survival 88% vs 47% (P=0.02); mRS 0-3 at 6-12 mo: 47% vs 27% (P=0.23) — primary endpoint not significant alone
trials.teachingPoint: Demonstrated the survival benefit of hemicraniectomy in malignant MCA infarction; functional benefit established in the pooled analysis.

trials.name: HAMLET
trials.fullName: Hemicraniectomy After Middle Cerebral Artery Infarction with Life-threatening Edema Trial
trials.population: n=64, adults, NIHSS space-occupying hemispheric infarction, randomized within 4 days of onset
trials.finding: No effect on primary outcome (ARR 0%, 95% CI −21 to 21); case fatality reduced (ARR 38%, 95% CI 15-60)
trials.teachingPoint: Operate within 48 h: delayed decompression saves lives but has no demonstrated functional benefit.

trials.name: DESTINY II
trials.fullName: Hemicraniectomy in Older Patients with Extensive Middle-Cerebral-Artery Stroke
trials.population: n=112, ≥61 (median 70, range 61-82), NIHSS malignant MCA infarction, randomized within 48 h of onset
trials.finding: Favored surgery: 38% vs 18%
trials.teachingPoint: Hemicraniectomy improves survival without severe disability in patients >60, at the cost of survival largely into mRS 4-5.

trials.name: TEMPO-2
trials.fullName: Tenecteplase versus Standard of Care for Minor Ischaemic Stroke with Proven Occlusion (TEMPO-2)
trials.population: n=886, adults, NIHSS 0-5 (minor), ≤12 h
trials.finding: No benefit: 72% (309/432) tenecteplase vs 75% (338/452) control
trials.teachingPoint: Argues against routine thrombolysis for minor non-disabling stroke solely because an occlusion is present; keep the disabling-deficit gate.

trials.name: ARAMIS
trials.fullName: Dual Antiplatelet Therapy vs Alteplase for Patients With Minor Nondisabling Acute Ischemic Stroke
trials.population: n=760, median 64 (IQR 57-71); 31.0% women, NIHSS NIHSS ≤5, with ≤1 point on key single items (median 2), ≤4.5 h
trials.finding: Non-inferior: 93.8% (DAPT) vs 91.4% (alteplase)
trials.teachingPoint: For genuinely non-disabling minor stroke within 4.5 h, DAPT is a reasonable alternative to IV thrombolysis.

trials.name: INTREPID
trials.fullName: Fever Prevention in Patients With Acute Vascular Brain Injury
trials.population: n=677, median 62; 51% female, NIHSS critically ill: 254 ischemic stroke, 223 ICH, 200 SAH, up to 14 days or ICU discharge
trials.finding: Fever burden markedly reduced — prevention is achievable
trials.teachingPoint: Device-based fever prevention reduced fever burden but did not improve 3-month function; halted for futility.

trials.name: SETPOINT2
trials.fullName: Early vs Standard Approach to Tracheostomy in Severe Stroke Receiving Mechanical Ventilation
trials.population: n=382, median 59; 49.8% women, NIHSS severe acute ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke requiring invasive ventilation, 6-month outcome
trials.finding: No significant benefit from early tracheostomy
trials.teachingPoint: Early (<=5 day) tracheostomy did not improve 6-month outcome in ventilated severe stroke; a third of controls avoided tracheostomy entirely.

trials.name: RAISE
trials.fullName: Reteplase versus Alteplase for Acute Ischemic Stroke
trials.population: n=1412, adults, NIHSS IVT-eligible, ≤4.5 h
trials.finding: Superior: 79.5% (reteplase) vs 70.4% (alteplase)
trials.teachingPoint: Reteplase beat alteplase for mRS 0-1 within 4.5 h but with more ICH overall; not a default agent outside the trial setting.

trials.name: Save ChildS
trials.fullName: Feasibility, Safety, and Outcome of Endovascular Recanalization in Childhood Stroke: The Save ChildS Study
trials.population: n=73, Under 18 years; median age 11.3 years (IQR 7.0-15.0). 37 (51%) boys and 36 (49%) girls, NIHSS Median Pediatric NIH Stroke Scale (PedNIHSS) 14.0 (IQR 9.2-20.0) at admission, on a scale of 0 (no deficit) to 34 (maximum deficit), Cases accrued 1 January 2000 to 31 December 2018; median follow-up 16 months. No uniform time-from-onset window was applied — treatment timing was at the discretion of the treating centre
trials.finding: Neurologic status improved: median PedNIHSS fell from 14.0 (IQR 9.2-20.0) at admission to 4.0 (IQR 2.0-7.3) at day 7. With no control arm, this is a description of outcome after treatment, not a treatment effect.
trials.teachingPoint: Frames pediatric thrombectomy honestly: feasible, with complication rates not detectably worse than in adult trials, but supported only by a 73-child uncontrolled series because the sole randomized pediatric thrombolysis trial closed after enrolling one child — so it remains an off-label, case-by-case extrapolation from adult evidence.

trials.name: RESPECT
trials.fullName: Long-Term Outcomes of Patent Foramen Ovale Closure or Medical Therapy after Stroke
trials.finding: Favored closure: 0.58 vs 1.07 per 100 pt-yr
trials.teachingPoint: Long-term PFO closure reduces recurrent stroke vs medical therapy in selected patients <60 y.

trials.name: CLOSE
trials.fullName: Patent Foramen Ovale Closure or Anticoagulation vs Antiplatelets after Stroke
trials.finding: Favored closure: 0/238 vs 14/235
trials.teachingPoint: Closure markedly cuts recurrent stroke in high-risk PFO anatomy (ASA / large shunt).

trials.name: REDUCE
trials.fullName: Patent Foramen Ovale Closure or Antiplatelet Therapy for Cryptogenic Stroke
trials.finding: Favored closure: 1.4% vs 5.4%
trials.teachingPoint: Closure reduces recurrent stroke and new infarcts; watch for AF and device events.

trials.name: Finnish Subsequent-Pregnancy Cohort
trials.fullName: Stroke Recurrence and Pregnancy Outcomes in the Subsequent Pregnancies After Maternal Ischemic Stroke
trials.population: n=90, Women of reproductive age who sustained an ischemic stroke during pregnancy or the puerperium, NIHSS Not reported as NIHSS, Index strokes occurred in Finland 1987-2016; subsequent pregnancies followed thereafter through national registers
trials.finding: Women with a prior maternal ischemic stroke were LESS likely to have any subsequent pregnancy: 38.9% versus 51.7% of controls, age-adjusted OR 0.55. Among those who did conceive again, three women had a recurrent maternal ischemic stroke or transient ischemic attack — reported as 8.6%, which is 3 events among the roughly 35 women who had a subsequent pregnancy, NOT 3 of 90. With three events, this figure is an order-of-magnitude estimate only.
trials.teachingPoint: Supplies the first numbers for counselling after a pregnancy-associated ischemic stroke: most subsequent pregnancies proceed, but they behave as high-risk pregnancies warranting planned antithrombotic continuation, blood-pressure surveillance and glucose screening.

trials.name: INTERACT4
trials.fullName: Intensive Ambulance-Delivered Blood-Pressure Reduction in Hyperacute Stroke
trials.population: n=2404, mean age 70, NIHSS suspected stroke with motor deficit, ≤2 h from onset, assessed in the ambulance
trials.finding: Neutral overall: no difference in functional outcome
trials.teachingPoint: Do not lower BP prehospital in undifferentiated stroke — benefit in hemorrhage is offset by harm in ischemia. Supports imaging-first BP decisions.

trials.name: BEST-MSU
trials.fullName: Prospective, Multicenter, Controlled Trial of Mobile Stroke Units
trials.population: n=1515, adults, NIHSS all; 1047 were tPA-eligible, ≤4.5 h from onset
trials.finding: Favors MSU: mean uw-mRS 0.72 vs 0.66
trials.teachingPoint: Mobile stroke units improved 90-day disability outcomes vs standard EMS, via faster and more complete thrombolysis delivery.

trials.name: RACECAT
trials.fullName: Direct Transportation to a Thrombectomy-Capable Center vs Local Stroke Center in Suspected Large-Vessel Occlusion in Nonurban Areas
trials.population: n=1401, median 75 (IQR 65-83); 56% men, NIHSS median NIHSS 17 (IQR 11-21), prehospital, nonurban Catalonia
trials.finding: Neutral: median mRS 3 in both arms
trials.teachingPoint: In nonurban areas, direct transport to a thrombectomy centre did not improve 90-day outcome versus the nearest stroke centre.

trials.name: VNS-REHAB
trials.fullName: Vagus Nerve Stimulation Paired with Rehabilitation for Upper Limb Motor Function after Ischaemic Stroke
trials.population: n=108, adults, NIHSS moderate-to-severe arm weakness (baseline Fugl-Meyer Upper Extremity 20-50), at least 9 months after ischemic stroke — the CHRONIC phase
trials.finding: Favors paired VNS
trials.teachingPoint: Paired vagus nerve stimulation improved chronic post-stroke upper-limb impairment versus sham in a rigorous implanted-control design.

trials.name: RESIST
trials.fullName: Remote Ischemic Conditioning for Acute Stroke: The RESIST Randomized Clinical Trial
trials.population: n=1500, Median 71 y; 591 (41%) women, NIHSS Not reported in the abstract — patients were enrolled prehospital on symptoms alone, before any diagnostic imaging, Prehospital stroke symptoms for less than 4 h
trials.finding: DID NOT meet: median mRS 2 (IQR 1-3) with RIC vs 1 (IQR 1-3) with sham — RIC was not associated with improved functional outcome
trials.teachingPoint: Ambulance-initiated remote ischemic conditioning does not improve 90-day outcome and is not a prehospital intervention to adopt.

trials.name: RICAMIS
trials.fullName: Effect of Remote Ischemic Conditioning vs Usual Care on Neurologic Function in Patients With Acute Moderate Ischemic Stroke: The RICAMIS Randomized Clinical Trial
trials.population: n=1893, Mean 65 y (SD 10.3); 606 (34.1%) women, NIHSS Acute moderate ischaemic stroke (the trial's severity band; the abstract does not give the numeric NIHSS range or median), Randomised within 48 h of symptom onset
trials.finding: MET: mRS 0-1 in 582 (67.4%) with RIC vs 566 (62.0%) with usual care — an absolute difference of 5.4 percentage points
trials.teachingPoint: Shows a 5.4-point absolute gain in excellent outcome with RIC in moderate stroke, but from an unblinded usual-care comparison the authors themselves say needs replication.

trials.name: SERIC-EVT
trials.fullName: Remote ischaemic conditioning improves outcomes of ischaemic stroke treated by endovascular thrombectomy: the SERIC-EVT trial
trials.population: n=498, Not reported in the abstract, NIHSS Not reported in the abstract, After endovascular thrombectomy for acute large-vessel occlusion
trials.finding: MET: mRS 0-2 in 61.1% with RIC vs 48.9% with sham RIC — note that the effect estimate reported in the abstract is UNADJUSTED
trials.teachingPoint: The first sham-controlled evidence that RIC after thrombectomy may improve 90-day independence — promising enough to justify confirmatory trials, not enough to change practice.

trials.name: EnTRIPS
trials.fullName: Remote Ischemic Postconditioning in Endovascular Thrombectomy for Stroke: The EnTRIPS Randomized Clinical Trial
trials.population: n=270, Mean 65.5 y (SD 16.8); 171 (63.8%) men, NIHSS Not reported in the abstract, Presentation within 24 h of onset; conditioning randomised and started within 6 h AFTER endovascular treatment
trials.finding: DID NOT meet: mRS 0-2 in 81/133 (60.9%) with RIPC vs 78/135 (57.8%) with control — no significant improvement in 90-day functional outcome
trials.teachingPoint: Ultra-early remote ischemic postconditioning after successful thrombectomy was safe but showed no functional benefit, so the RIC-after-EVT question remains open rather than answered.

trials.name: SAHaRA
trials.fullName: Liberal or Restrictive Transfusion Strategy in Aneurysmal Subarachnoid Hemorrhage
trials.population: n=742, critically ill adults, NIHSS all clinical grades, critical-care period after aSAH
trials.finding: Neutral: 33.5% vs 37.7%
trials.teachingPoint: A liberal (Hgb ≤10) transfusion threshold after aSAH did not improve 12-month outcome — restrictive transfusion remains reasonable.

trials.name: ULTRA
trials.fullName: Ultra-Early Tranexamic Acid After Subarachnoid Haemorrhage
trials.population: n=955, adults, NIHSS all grades, immediately after diagnosis, until aneurysm treatment or 24 h
trials.finding: Neutral: 60% vs 64%
trials.teachingPoint: Routine ultra-early tranexamic acid is not indicated in aSAH — prioritise early aneurysm securing instead.

trials.name: EARLYDRAIN
trials.fullName: Effectiveness of Lumbar Cerebrospinal Fluid Drain Among Patients With Aneurysmal Subarachnoid Hemorrhage
trials.population: n=287, median 55 (IQR 48-63); 68.6% female, NIHSS all clinical grades, lumbar drain started within 72 h of SAH, after aneurysm securing within 48 h
trials.finding: Favors lumbar drain: 32.6% vs 44.8%
trials.teachingPoint: Prophylactic early lumbar drainage after aneurysm securing reduced secondary infarction and unfavorable 6-month outcome.

trials.name: MATCH
trials.fullName: Aspirin and Clopidogrel Compared with Clopidogrel Alone after Recent Ischaemic Stroke or TIA in High-Risk Patients
trials.population: n=7599, adults, NIHSS recent ischemic stroke or TIA plus ≥1 additional vascular risk factor, 18 months of treatment and follow-up
trials.finding: Neutral: 15.7% vs 16.7%
trials.teachingPoint: Adding aspirin to clopidogrel for 18 months after stroke/TIA gave no significant benefit and doubled life-threatening bleeding.

trials.name: SAVE
trials.fullName: Sleep Apnea Cardiovascular Endpoints — CPAP for Prevention of Cardiovascular Events in Obstructive Sleep Apnea (SAVE)
trials.population: n=2717, 45-75 years; most participants were men, NIHSS not reported — enrolment was by established coronary or cerebrovascular disease, not stroke severity, mean follow-up 3.7 years
trials.finding: DID NOT meet: a primary end-point event occurred in 229 CPAP participants (17.0%) and 207 usual-care participants (15.4%) — the point estimate favors usual care
trials.teachingPoint: Teaches that CPAP should be offered for symptoms — sleepiness, snoring, quality of life — and not promised as a way to prevent recurrent vascular events; the largest randomized test found no event reduction.

trials.name: Post-stroke PAP meta-analysis
trials.fullName: Post-stroke sleep disordered breathing and the effect of positive airway pressure treatment: an updated systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
trials.population: n=1457, not reported in the abstract, NIHSS not reported in the abstract, records searched from inception in July 2024 up to September 2024; 72,387 records screened
trials.finding: PAP reduced recurrent vascular events
trials.teachingPoint: Keeps the post-stroke sleep-apnea question open rather than closing it: a pooled signal for fewer recurrent vascular events sits against a larger neutral trial, and neither supports promising a patient that PAP will improve functional independence.

trials.name: Suicide after stroke
trials.fullName: Increased Risk of Suicide after Stroke: A Population-Based Matched Cohort Study
trials.finding: Higher in stroke survivors: 11.1 vs 3.2 per 10,000 person-years
trials.teachingPoint: Supports long-term (beyond 1 year) suicidality screening in survivors — especially younger and lower-income patients.

trials.name: QASC
trials.fullName: Quality in Acute Stroke Care: implementation of evidence-based treatment protocols to manage fever, hyperglycaemia, and swallowing dysfunction in acute stroke
trials.population: n=1696, adults ≥18 y, NIHSS unselected stroke severity; benefit reported as present irrespective of severity, presentation ≤48 h of symptom onset
trials.finding: POSITIVE: intervention-unit patients were significantly less likely to be dead or dependent — 236/558 (42%) vs 259/449 (58%) — number needed to treat 6.4
trials.teachingPoint: Supports enforcing a nurse-initiated fever/glucose/swallowing protocol on admission as a package rather than leaving each element to individual discretion.

trials.name: CLOTS 3
trials.fullName: Effectiveness of intermittent pneumatic compression in reduction of risk of deep vein thrombosis in patients who have had a stroke (CLOTS 3)
trials.population: n=2876, median 76 y (IQR 67-84), NIHSS not reported; immobility used as the entry criterion instead of NIHSS, enrolled day 0 to day 3 of hospital admission
trials.finding: POSITIVE: proximal DVT in 122/1438 (8.5%) with IPC vs 174/1438 (12.1%) without — absolute risk reduction 3.6%
trials.teachingPoint: Supports applying intermittent pneumatic compression from the day of admission in stroke patients who cannot walk to the toilet unaided, with daily skin inspection.

trials.name: CLOTS 1
trials.fullName: Effectiveness of thigh-length graduated compression stockings to reduce the risk of deep vein thrombosis after stroke (CLOTS trial 1)
trials.population: n=2518, adults; trial enrolled a broadly representative immobile stroke population, NIHSS not reported; immobility used as the entry criterion, admitted to hospital within 1 week of acute stroke
trials.finding: DID NOT meet its aim — NULL: proximal DVT in 126/1256 (10.0%) with stockings vs 133/1262 (10.5%) without, a non-significant absolute risk reduction of 0.5%
trials.teachingPoint: Argues against ordering thigh-length graduated compression stockings for VTE prophylaxis after stroke, given no measured benefit and a four-fold excess of skin injury.

trials.name: PREVAIL
trials.fullName: The efficacy and safety of enoxaparin versus unfractionated heparin for the prevention of venous thromboembolism after acute ischaemic stroke (PREVAIL Study)
trials.population: n=1762, adults, NIHSS stratified at randomisation: severe stroke NIHSS ≥14 vs less severe NIHSS <14, randomised within 48 h of symptom onset
trials.finding: POSITIVE for the composite: 68/666 (10%) with enoxaparin vs 121/669 (18%) with unfractionated heparin — a 43% relative reduction
trials.teachingPoint: Informs the choice between once-daily enoxaparin and twice-daily unfractionated heparin for VTE prophylaxis in non-ambulatory ischaemic stroke, with extracranial bleeding as the trade-off to weigh.

trials.name: FOOD (Trials 2 and 3)
trials.fullName: Effect of timing and method of enteral tube feeding for dysphagic stroke patients (FOOD): a multicentre randomised controlled trial
trials.population: n=1180, adults admitted with stroke and dysphagia, NIHSS not reported; dysphagia requiring consideration of tube feeding was the entry criterion, Trial 2 enrolled within 7 days of admission; Trial 3 within 30 days of admission
trials.finding: BOTH comparisons DID NOT meet significance on the primary endpoint. Trial 2 (early vs avoid): absolute reduction in death of 5.8% (p=0.09, not significant) but a reduction in death or poor outcome of only 1.2% (p=0.7) — i.e. the primary endpoint was flat, with the direction of effect being fewer deaths and more dependent survivors. Trial 3 (PEG vs nasogastric): absolute INCREASE in risk of death of 1.0% (p=0.9) and an increased risk of death or poor outcome of 7.8% (p=0.05), i.e. borderline evidence of harm from starting with PEG
trials.teachingPoint: Frames tube-feeding decisions after stroke as a survival-versus-dependency trade-off and argues against starting with a PEG rather than a nasogastric tube in newly dysphagic patients.

trials.name: SO2S
trials.fullName: Effect of Routine Low-Dose Oxygen Supplementation on Death and Disability in Adults With Acute Stroke: The Stroke Oxygen Study Randomized Clinical Trial
trials.population: n=8003, mean 72 y (SD 13); 4398 (55%) men, NIHSS median NIHSS 5 — a predominantly mild stroke population, enrolled within 24 h of hospital admission
trials.finding: DID NOT meet — NULL: no benefit of prophylactic oxygen at any dose or schedule. Unadjusted OR for a better outcome 0.97 for oxygen vs control, and 1.03 for continuous vs nocturnal oxygen. No subgroup could be identified that benefited
trials.teachingPoint: Argues against routine prophylactic supplemental oxygen in non-hypoxic stroke patients; treat the measured desaturation, not the diagnosis.

trials.name: HeadPoST
trials.fullName: Head Positioning in Acute Stroke Trial: cluster-randomized, crossover trial of head positioning in acute stroke
trials.population: n=11093, adults with acute stroke, NIHSS not reported in the primary publication abstract; 85% of strokes were ischaemic, position initiated soon after hospital admission; median 14 h from symptom onset (IQR 5-35 h) and maintained for 24 h
trials.finding: DID NOT meet — NULL: no significant shift in the 90-day mRS distribution between lying flat and sitting up
trials.teachingPoint: Removes routine head-of-bed position from the list of things that change stroke outcome, leaving it a patient-specific judgement about perfusion or aspiration risk.

trials.name: PASS
trials.fullName: The Preventive Antibiotics in Stroke Study (PASS): a pragmatic randomised open-label masked endpoint clinical trial
trials.population: n=2550, adults with acute stroke, NIHSS not reported in the primary publication abstract, randomised within 24 h of symptom onset
trials.finding: DID NOT meet — NULL: preventive ceftriaxone did not affect the distribution of 90-day mRS scores
trials.teachingPoint: Argues against prophylactic antibiotics as part of the stroke admission bundle; antibiotics are for documented infection.

trials.name: SHINE
trials.fullName: Stroke Hyperglycemia Insulin Network Effort (SHINE): Intensive vs Standard Treatment of Hyperglycemia and Functional Outcome in Patients With Acute Ischemic Stroke
trials.population: n=1151, mean 66 y (SD 13.1); 529 (46%) women, NIHSS not reported in the primary publication abstract; the primary outcome was adjusted for baseline stroke severity, enrolled within 12 h of stroke onset; treatment for up to 72 h
trials.finding: DID NOT meet — NULL, and enrolment was STOPPED FOR FUTILITY at a prespecified interim analysis: favourable outcome in 119/581 (20.5%) with intensive control vs 123/570 (21.6%) with standard control
trials.teachingPoint: Argues against intensive IV insulin targeting 80-130 mg/dL after ischaemic stroke; a moderate target avoids the hypoglycaemia without giving up any measured functional benefit.

trials.name: AVERT dose-response
trials.fullName: Prespecified dose-response analysis for A Very Early Rehabilitation Trial (AVERT)
trials.population: n=2104, aged ≥18 y, NIHSS baseline stroke severity was a modelled covariate and a top CART splitting variable; range not stated in the abstract, admitted to a stroke unit within 24 h of stroke onset
trials.finding: The two dose dimensions pull in OPPOSITE directions: greater daily frequency of out-of-bed sessions improved the odds of a favourable outcome (OR 1.13), while greater amount of mobilisation in minutes per day REDUCED the odds of a good outcome (OR 0.94), each holding the other and time to first mobilisation constant
trials.teachingPoint: Supports framing early mobilisation orders around short, frequent out-of-bed sessions rather than total minutes, while flagging that the randomised dose question was not settled by this analysis.

trials.name: ARTESiA
trials.fullName: Apixaban for Stroke Prevention in Subclinical Atrial Fibrillation
trials.population: n=4012, ≥55, NIHSS n/a, subclinical AF detected on device
trials.finding: Favored apixaban: 0.78%/y vs 1.24%/y
trials.teachingPoint: Establishes apixaban benefit in subclinical AF; the ICH-survivor question is addressed by PRESTIGE-AF, SoSTART, APACHE-AF and the COCROACH meta-analysis, which enrolled that population.

trials.name: NOAH-AFNET 6
trials.fullName: Anticoagulation with Edoxaban in Patients with Atrial High-Rate Episodes
trials.population: n=2536, mean 78; 37.4% women, NIHSS device-detected atrial high-rate episodes ≥6 min, median duration 2.8 h, median follow-up 21 months (terminated early)
trials.finding: Neutral: 3.2%/patient-year vs 4.0%/patient-year
trials.teachingPoint: Edoxaban for device-detected AHRE did not reduce cardiovascular events and increased death or major bleeding; stroke risk was ~1%/year untreated.

trials.name: LOOP
trials.fullName: Implantable Loop Recorder Detection of Atrial Fibrillation to Prevent Stroke
trials.population: n=6004, 70-90 (mean 74.7); 47.3% women, NIHSS no known AF, ≥1 stroke risk factor (90.7% hypertensive), median follow-up 64.5 months
trials.finding: Neutral: 4.5% vs 5.6%
trials.teachingPoint: Loop-recorder AF screening tripled detection but did not significantly reduce stroke — detection alone is not a surrogate for benefit.

trials.name: GWTG-Stroke door-in-door-out
trials.fullName: Door-in-Door-out Times for Interhospital Transfer of Patients With Stroke (Get With The Guidelines-Stroke registry analysis)
trials.population: n=108913, mean 66.7 y (SD 15.2); 50.6% male; 71.7% non-Hispanic White, NIHSS full range; NIHSS >12 vs 0-1 was one of the strongest correlates of a shorter door-in-door-out time, emergency-department stay at the transferring hospital, January 2019 to December 2021
trials.finding: Real-world practice falls well short of the benchmark: median door-in-door-out time 174 minutes (IQR 116-276), and only 29,741 of 108,913 patients (27.3%) were transferred within 120 minutes
trials.teachingPoint: Gives transfer decisions a concrete, measurable benchmark — a ≤120-minute door-in-door-out target that most US transfers currently miss — and names EMS prenotification and demographic disparity as the levers to audit.

trials.name: Target Stroke Phase III
trials.fullName: Association of Component Strategies of the Target Stroke Phase 3 Nationwide Quality Improvement Program With Accelerated Door-to-Puncture and Door-In-Door-Out Times for Ischemic Stroke Endovascular Thrombectomy in the United States
trials.population: n=0, adults; the total cohort size is NOT stated in the retrieved abstract, so no n is asserted here, NIHSS not reported in the retrieved abstract, 1 January 2017 to 31 March 2022
trials.finding: Different strategies work at different points in the chain. In DIRECT-ARRIVING EVT patients, two strategies were independently associated with shorter door-to-puncture time: alerting the neurointerventional team on EMS prenotification (−21.9 minutes) and performing CT plus CTA in all patients presenting ≤24 h from last known well (−6.6 minutes). In TRANSFER-IN EVT patients, two different strategies helped: greater use of stroke screening tools (−3.5 minutes per 25% increase in use) and greater use of a camera during telestroke consultations (−5.8 minutes per 25% increase in camera use)
trials.teachingPoint: Identifies which workflow changes are associated with faster reperfusion at each node of a transfer network — team activation on prenotification at the hub, screening tools and telestroke cameras at the spoke.

trials.name: AI LVO-detection accuracy meta-analysis
trials.fullName: Diagnostic Test Accuracy of Artificial Intelligence in Large Vessel Occlusion: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
trials.population: n=10937, not reported at the pooled level, NIHSS not reported at the pooled level, acute stroke CT angiography at presentation
trials.finding: Accuracy is good but asymmetric, and the negative result is the weak one: pooled sensitivity 0.87 and pooled specificity 0.95. The pooled positive likelihood ratio was 9.55 and statistically significant, while the pooled negative likelihood ratio of 0.14 was NOT statistically significant — meaning a negative AI read does not reliably rule out an occlusion
trials.teachingPoint: Frames AI LVO-detection output as a rule-in aid that can speed a transfer, never a rule-out that can cancel one — especially for posterior-circulation and M2 occlusions.

trials.name: CERES-TANDEM
trials.fullName: Emergent Carotid Stenting for Acute Anterior Circulation Ischemic Stroke With Tandem Lesions: The Multicenter CERES-TANDEM Study
trials.population: n=4053, mean 70 y; 65.5% female, NIHSS Not specified in the abstract, Within 24 h of symptom onset (presentation beyond 24 h was an exclusion)
trials.finding: Emergent carotid stenting was ASSOCIATED WITH a better mRS shift after IPTW weighting
trials.teachingPoint: Provides the largest real-world signal that stenting the cervical carotid during thrombectomy for a tandem lesion tracks with better 90-day recovery without more symptomatic haemorrhage — an association to weigh, not a randomized result to follow.

trials.name: IRIS tandem-lesion carotid-stenting analysis
trials.fullName: Acute Carotid Stenting for Tandem Lesions in Patients Randomized to Endovascular Treatment With or Without Thrombolysis: Results From the IRIS Individual Participant Data Meta-Analysis
trials.population: n=340, Not specified in the abstract, NIHSS Not specified in the abstract, Per the contributing trials; all patients presented directly to endovascular-capable centres
trials.finding: Acute carotid stenting was ASSOCIATED WITH better 90-day functional outcomes; confirmed on inverse-probability-of-treatment weighting (adjusted common OR 1.66, 95% CI 1.08-2.54)
trials.teachingPoint: Teaches that prior IV thrombolysis did not modify the association between acute carotid stenting and 90-day outcome in tandem lesions — evidence against treating a preceding lytic as an automatic contraindication to stenting, while the randomized question remains open.

trials.name: AcT
trials.fullName: Intravenous Tenecteplase Compared with Alteplase for Acute Ischaemic Stroke in Canada
trials.finding: Non-inferior: 36.9% (TNK) vs 34.8% (alteplase)
trials.teachingPoint: Supports TNK 0.25 mg/kg as a preferred IV thrombolytic for IVT-eligible AIS within 4.5 h.

trials.name: TRACE-2
trials.fullName: Trial of Tenecteplase in Chinese Patients with Acute Ischemic Stroke
trials.finding: Non-inferior: 62.0% (TNK) vs 58.0% (alteplase)
trials.teachingPoint: Confirms non-inferiority of TNK in non-LVO eligible AIS within 4.5 h.

trials.name: ORIGINAL
trials.fullName: Tenecteplase vs Alteplase in AIS (ORIGINAL)
trials.finding: Non-inferior
trials.teachingPoint: Adds further RCT support for TNK as alteplase-equivalent first-line.

trials.name: TNK vs alteplase · RWE
trials.fullName: Real-World Efficacy and Safety of Tenecteplase versus Alteplase in Acute Ischemic Stroke: A Propensity Score-Matched Analysis
trials.finding: Comparable (p>0.05)
trials.teachingPoint: Adds real-world support for tenecteplase as a practical alteplase alternative — consistent with trial-level non-inferiority.

trials.name: BRIDGE-TNK
trials.fullName: Intravenous Tenecteplase before Thrombectomy in Stroke
trials.population: n=550, adults, ≤4.5 h
trials.finding: Favored TNK + thrombectomy: 52.9% vs 44.1%
trials.teachingPoint: Reinforces bridging IV thrombolysis before thrombectomy for eligible LVO within 4.5 h; do not routinely skip IVT in thrombolysis-eligible patients headed to EVT inside that window. Says nothing about later windows.

trials.name: TASTE
trials.fullName: Tenecteplase versus Alteplase for Thrombolysis in Patients Selected by Perfusion Imaging within 4.5 h
trials.population: n=680, median 74 (IQR 63-82); 38% female, NIHSS median NIHSS 7 (IQR 4-11), ≤4.5 h from onset or last known well
trials.finding: Non-inferiority met per-protocol (59% vs 56%) but NOT in intention-to-treat (57% vs 55%)
trials.teachingPoint: Adds perfusion-selected, multi-country support for TNK 0.25 mg/kg, and shows large-scale CTP-guided IVT selection is feasible.

trials.name: PHASES
trials.fullName: Development of the PHASES Score for Prediction of Risk of Rupture of Intracranial Aneurysms
trials.population: n=8382, adults across six prospective cohorts, NIHSS incidental unruptured saccular aneurysms, 29,166 person-years of follow-up
trials.finding: Mean 1-year rupture risk 1.4%; 5-year risk 3.4% (230 ruptures)
trials.teachingPoint: PHASES gives an absolute 5-year rupture risk for incidental aneurysms, anchoring treat-versus-observe discussions.

trials.name: INVICTUS
trials.fullName: Rivaroxaban in Rheumatic Heart Disease-Associated Atrial Fibrillation
trials.population: n=4531, mean 50.5; 72.3% women, NIHSS AF with echocardiographic rheumatic heart disease, restricted mean survival analysis over ~4.6 years
trials.finding: VKA SUPERIOR: restricted mean survival 1599 d (rivaroxaban) vs 1675 d (VKA)
trials.teachingPoint: Use warfarin, not a DOAC, for AF with rheumatic mitral valve disease — rivaroxaban had worse cardiovascular outcomes and higher mortality.

trials.name: WAKE-UP
trials.fullName: MRI-Guided Thrombolysis for Stroke with Unknown Time of Onset
trials.population: n=503, 18-80, NIHSS NIHSS ≤25, unknown onset (last seen well >4.5 h)
trials.finding: Favored alteplase: 53.3% vs 41.8%
trials.teachingPoint: Foundational evidence for imaging-selected thrombolysis in wake-up / unknown onset stroke.

trials.name: TWIST
trials.fullName: Tenecteplase in Wake-up Ischaemic Stroke Trial
trials.population: n=578, ≥18, wake-up <4.5 h after waking
trials.finding: No significant benefit overall
trials.teachingPoint: Late-window thrombolysis without advanced imaging is not supported.

trials.name: Jefferson Inherited Thrombophilia Audit
trials.fullName: Low value of inherited thrombophilia testing among patients with stroke or transient ischemic attack: A three-year retrospective study
trials.population: n=249, Median age 49.0 years; 50.2% female, NIHSS Not reported as NIHSS; the cohort comprises isolated acute ischemic stroke or TIA, including branch and central retinal artery occlusion, Testing performed during the index hospital admission; admissions 1 January 2019 to 31 December 2021
trials.finding: HIGH ABNORMAL RATE, ZERO MANAGEMENT IMPACT. 42.2% of patients had at least one abnormal test and 14.3% of the 1035 individual tests resulted abnormal — but 28% of abnormal results were borderline positive antigen or activity assays that likely represented false positives, and NO patient with an abnormal result had their clinical management changed as a result. Charges for the tests totalled $468,588 USD.
trials.teachingPoint: Argues against reflexively ordering an inpatient inherited thrombophilia panel after an isolated arterial ischemic stroke or TIA — the yield is high in abnormal results, substantially false-positive, and in this audit changed management in no one; acquired antiphospholipid testing is a separate question.

trials.name: sifap
trials.fullName: Stroke in Young Fabry Patients (sifap): acute cerebrovascular disease in the young
trials.population: n=5023, 18 to 55 years; median age 46. Males predominated overall (2962, 59%), but females outnumbered males (65.3%) in the youngest band, aged 18-24, NIHSS Not reported as NIHSS; the cohort comprised 3396 ischemic strokes, 271 hemorrhagic strokes and 1071 transient ischemic attacks, Enrolled at the acute event; recruitment April 2007 to January 2010
trials.finding: LOW BUT NON-TRIVIAL YIELD: definite Fabry disease was diagnosed in 0.5% (95% CI 0.4%-0.8%, n=27) of all patients, with probable Fabry disease in a further 18 patients (0.4%). Roughly 1 in 200 young stroke patients had definite Fabry disease. The figure depends on the study's own definite-versus-probable classification algorithm, so it is best used as an order-of-magnitude prevalence rather than a precise rate.
trials.teachingPoint: Supports phenotype-driven rather than universal Fabry screening in young stroke — about 1 in 200 young stroke patients has definite Fabry disease — while showing that large-artery atherosclerosis and dissection, not rare diseases, dominate the causes of stroke between 18 and 55.

trials.name: UKYSS
trials.fullName: Demographics, risk factor profiles and etiologies in young ischemic and hemorrhagic stroke — the United Kingdom Young Stroke Study (UKYSS)
trials.population: n=1765, Mean age 41.6 years (SD 7.1), NIHSS Not reported as NIHSS in the abstract, First-ever stroke; ambispective observational data collection
trials.finding: DESCRIPTIVE, and the headline is how conventional young stroke turns out to be. Among ischemic strokes, 50.8% (723) were classified cryptogenic and 38.1% (542) hypertensive. Only 13.4% (191) of the whole cohort received intravenous thrombolysis and 5% (71) mechanical thrombectomy. Among hemorrhagic strokes, hypertension was both the commonest risk factor (56.6%, 192) and the commonest etiology (49.6%, 168), and 15.3% (52) underwent neurosurgery.
trials.teachingPoint: Sets realistic expectations for the young-stroke workup: half of young ischemic strokes remain cryptogenic, hypertension is the single most common modifiable factor across both ischemic and hemorrhagic young stroke, and by the late forties the risk-factor profile is already conventional.

trials.name: Illicit Drug Use and Stroke (meta-analysis + Mendelian randomization)
trials.fullName: Does illicit drug use increase stroke risk? A systematic review, meta-analyses, and Mendelian randomization analysis
trials.population: n=32, Not restricted by age; the observational component draws on administrative, hospital-based and population-based datasets totalling more than 100 million participants across 32 studies, NIHSS Not applicable, Studies from inception of the searched databases; PROSPERO registration CRD420251053702
trials.finding: POSITIVE for three of four drug classes: cannabis OR 1.37 (95% CI 1.14-1.65), cocaine OR 1.96 (95% CI 1.27-3.01) and amphetamines OR 2.22 (95% CI 1.40-3.53) were each significantly associated with increased stroke risk, while opioids showed NO significant association. The authors state explicitly that the cannabis finding showed heterogeneity and small-study effects, so it is the least secure of the three.
trials.teachingPoint: Supports routinely taking a substance-use history — and considering a toxicology screen — in young or cryptogenic stroke, since cocaine, amphetamine and cannabis exposure show concordant observational and genetic associations with stroke.
